As if a clear wine had appeared with naḥs,
Whose dew made the pure water appear.

It was also said: it was named so because it was full of dust, and from this is the rajaz poet's saying:

I set out before the rising of the sun
To hunt on a day of little naḥs.

He means: little dust.

Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and Qatadah said: they were consecutive days, from the last Wednesday of Shawwal to the next Wednesday.

al-Sudi said: the first of them was the morning of Sunday. al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas said: Friday. Yahya ibn Salam said: Sunday.

﴿لِنُذِيقَهم عَذابَ الخِزْيِ في الحَياةِ الدُّنْيا﴾: this is destruction. It was also read (litudhīqahum) with a tāʾ. al-Zamakhshari said: [the subject is] the wind, or the ill-omened days. He attributed the punishment to disgrace as the attribution of a qualified noun to its qualifier, not using another word that implies sharing and detail. As for the statement about ﴿ولَعَذابُ الآخِرَةِ﴾, it is a figurative attribution, or the description of the punishment as disgraceful is more emphatic than describing them with it. Do you not see the difference between your saying "he is a poet" and "he has the poetry of a poet"? He matched their arrogance with the punishment of disgrace, which is humiliation and abasement.

He began with the story of ʿAd because it is older in time, then mentioned Thamud, saying: ﴿وأمّا ثَمُودُ﴾. The majority read it in the nominative as diptote (mamnūʿ min al-ṣarf). Ibn Wathhab, al-Aʿmash, and Bakr ibn Habib read it as declinable (maṣrūfan). This is the reading of Ibn Wathhab and al-Aʿmash for (Thamūd) with tanwin throughout the Qur'an, except His saying ﴿وآتَيْنا ثَمُودَ النّاقَةَ﴾ [al-Isra: 59], because in the codex it is written without an alif. It was also read as (Thamūda) in the accusative, diptote, and al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, and al-Aʿmash read (Thamūdan) in the accusative with tanwin. al-Mufaddal related from ʿAsim both readings. End of his words.

﴿فَهَدَيْناهُمْ﴾: Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatadah, al-Sudi and Ibn Zayd said: We made clear to them.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: guidance here does not mean direction (irshad). al-Farra', followed by al-Zamakhshari, said: ﴿فَهَدَيْناهُمْ﴾ means: We showed them the path of error and of right guidance, as in His saying: ﴿وهَدَيْناهُ النَّجْدَيْنِ﴾ [al-Balad: 10].

﴿فاسْتَحَبُّوا العَمى عَلى الهُدى﴾: they chose entry into error over entry into right guidance.

(If you say:) Does not the meaning of "hadaytuhu" (I guided him) denote that guidance came to be in him, the evidence for which is your saying "hadaytuhu fa-htada" (I guided him, so he was guided), in the sense of attaining and achieving the desired goal, just as you say "radda'tuhu fa-rtada'a" (I deterred him, so he was deterred)? How, then, is it permissible to use it for mere indication (al-dalalah al-mujarradah)?

(I say:) It is for indicating that He enabled them and removed their excuses, so that they had no pretext or cause left. Thus it is as if He attained the desired end in them by bringing about what necessitates and entails it. End of quote. And this is according to the方法 of the Mu'tazilah.

Sufyan said: "da'awnahum" (we called them). Ibn Zayd said: "a'lamnahumu al-huda min al-dalal" (we made them know guidance from misguidance).

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "fa-istahabbu" is an expression for their acquiring blindness (by their own earning), otherwise it is by Allah's origination. And what indicates that it refers to their acquisition is His saying: "bi-ma kanu yaksibun" (for what they used to earn). End of quote.

Al-Hun: humiliation (al-hawan). The punishment is described by the verbal noun, or it is a substitute for it. Ibn Miqsam recited: "'adhab al-hawan" with a fatha on the ha' and an alif after the waw.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Even if there were in the Qur'an no proof against the Qadariyyah, who are the Magians of this Ummah, by the testimony of its Prophet, and he is sufficient as a witness, except this (verse), it would suffice as a proof." End of quote, in keeping with his habit of reviling the People of the Sunnah.

Then He reminded Quraysh of the salvation of those who believed and were God-fearing. It was said: among those who responded and were saved from the believers were Hud and Salih, and one hundred and ten persons.

[p. 489]

﴿But if they turn away, say: "I have warned you of a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of ʿAd and Thamud."﴾ ﴿When the messengers came to them from before them and from behind them, saying, "Worship none but God." They said, "Had our Lord willed, He would have sent down angels. So we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent."﴾ ﴿As for ʿAd, they were arrogant on earth without right and said, "Who is stronger than us in strength?" Did they not see that God, who created them, is stronger than them in strength? And they used to deny Our signs.﴾ ﴿So We sent upon them a furious wind during ill-omened days, that We might make them taste the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world. But the punishment of the Hereafter is more disgracing, and they will not be helped.﴾ ﴿As for Thamud, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance, so the thunderbolt of the humiliating punishment seized them for what they used to earn.﴾ ﴿And We saved those who believed and used to be God-fearing.﴾

﴿فَإنْ أعْرَضُوا﴾: a shift (iltifat) from the second-person address in His saying ﴿أئِنَّكم لَتَكْفُرُونَ﴾ [Fussilat: 9] to the third-person pronoun, as a turning away from addressing them, since they had already been reminded, with the proofs that call for their attention and faith, of the Oneness and the overwhelming power. ﴿فَقُلْ أنْذَرْتُكُمْ﴾ means: I have informed you. (ṣāʿiqatan) means: the descent of a thunderbolt. Qatadah said: a punishment like the punishment of ʿAd and Thamud.

al-Zamakhshari said: a punishment of severe impact, as if it were a thunderbolt.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿صاعِقَةً مِثْلَ صاعِقَةِ﴾, while Ibn al-Zubayr, al-Sulami, al-Nakhaʿi and Ibn Muhaysin read them without the alif in both places and with a sukun on the ʿayn. Its explanation has already been given at the beginning of al-Baqarah.

The ṣaʿqah is the single occurrence: one says ṣaʿaqathu al-ṣāʿiqah fa-ṣuʿiqa (the thunderbolt struck him so he was struck down), and it is of the pattern faʿala with a fatha on the ʿayn, so the passive is fuʿila with a kasra, like khadaʿathu fa-khudiʿa (he deceived him so he was deceived). (Idh) is governed by (ṣāʿiqatan), because its meaning is punishment.

﴿مِن بَيْنِ أيْدِيهِمْ ومِن خَلْفِهِمْ﴾: Ibn ʿAbbas said: i.e., before them and after them, that is, before Hud and Salih and after them both.

It was also said: [it refers to] those who were sent to their forefathers and those who were sent to them. So ﴿مِن بَيْنِ أيْدِيهِمْ﴾ means: from before them, and ﴿ومِن خَلْفِهِمْ﴾ means: the messengers who were present with them. Thus the pronoun in (min khalfihim) refers to the messengers. This was said by al-Dahhak, and al-Farra' followed him, and a similar view will come from al-Tabari.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: ﴿مِن بَيْنِ أيْدِيهِمْ﴾ means: they preceded in time, and their warning was connected to the lifetimes of ʿAd and Thamud, and by this connection the proof was established.

﴿ومِن خَلْفِهِمْ﴾ means: a messenger came to them after their existence in time had passed. From the whole expression comes the establishment of proof against them, in that the message and the warning reached them both through report and through direct encounter. End of his words, and this is an explanation of Ibn ʿAbbas's statement.

al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿مِن بَيْنِ أيْدِيهِمْ ومِن خَلْفِهِمْ﴾ means: they came to them from every side, exerted themselves with them, and applied every stratagem with them, yet they found from them only obstinacy and aversion, as God related about Satan: ﴿لَآتِيَنَّهم مِن بَيْنِ أيْدِيهِمْ ومِن خَلْفِهِمْ وعَنْ أيْمانِهِمْ وعَنْ شَمائِلِهِمْ﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 17], meaning: I will come to them from every direction, and I will apply every stratagem against them.

It is reported from al-Hasan: they warned them of God's deeds regarding the nations before them and of the punishment of the Hereafter; for when they warned them of that, they had brought them admonition from the direction of the past time and what occurred in it upon the disbelievers, and from the direction of the future and what would befall them. End of his words.

al-Tabari said: the pronoun in His saying ﴿ومِن خَلْفِهِمْ﴾ refers to the messengers, and in ﴿مِن بَيْنِ أيْدِيهِمْ﴾ it refers to the nations. This departs from the apparent sense by separating the pronouns and obscuring the meaning, for the sense would become: the messengers came to them from before them and came to them from behind the messengers, that is, from behind themselves. This meaning is not intelligible unless the pronoun in (khalfihim) refers to (al-rusul) verbally, while it refers to other messengers in meaning. So it is as if He said: the messengers came to them from before them and from behind other messengers. This is like their saying: "I have a dirham and half of it," meaning: and half of another dirham. This is far-fetched.

From among the destroyed nations, ʿAd and Thamud were singled out for mention because the Quraysh knew their situation, and because they had settled upon their lands, in Yemen and al-Hijr. al-Afwah al-Awdi said:

They became like Qil ibn ʿAnz among his tribe, when ʿAd was destroyed by that which it had done.
Or after him like Qudar, when peoples followed him in error; so they perished.

(An lā taʿbudū) may be an explanatory (an), because the coming of the messengers to them implies the sense of speech, meaning: they came to them addressing them. It may also be a lightened form of the heavy (anna), meaning: that do not worship, the governing particle being for the imperfect verb, and it is joined to the prohibition just as it is joined to illa, as in ﴿أنْ طَهِّرا﴾ [al-Baqarah: 125], and as in "I wrote to him with an qum" (that stand up). In this construction there is only the sense of prohibition. It is also permissible, though far-fetched, for (lā) to be a negation and (an) to be a governing particle for the verb; this was said by al-Hawfi, and he mentioned no other view. The object of (shāʾa) is omitted, and al-Zamakhshari estimated it as: had our Lord willed [p. 490] the sending of messengers, He would have sent down angels. End of his words.

I investigated what has come in the Qur'an and in Arabic speech of this construction, and I found that the omitted part is never anything other than the same as the answer, such as His saying: ﴿ولَوْ شاءَ اللَّهُ لَجَمَعَهم عَلى الهُدى﴾ [al-Anʿam: 35], meaning: had God willed to gather them upon guidance, He would have gathered them upon it. Similarly: ﴿لَوْ نَشاءُ لَجَعَلْناهُ حُطامًا﴾ [al-Waqiʿah: 65], ﴿لَوْ نَشاءُ جَعَلْناهُ أُجاجًا﴾ [al-Waqiʿah: 70], ﴿ولَوْ شاءَ رَبُّكَ لَآمَنَ﴾ [Yunus: 99], ﴿ولَوْ شاءَ رَبُّكَ ما فَعَلُوهُ﴾ [al-Anʿam: 112], ﴿لَوْ شاءَ اللَّهُ ما عَبَدْنا مِن دُونِهِ مِن شَيْءٍ﴾ [al-Nahl: 35]. The poet said:

Had my Lord willed, I would have been Qays ibn Khalid,
And had my Lord willed, I would have been ʿUmar ibn Marthad.

The rajaz poet said:

And one who, had he willed, would have been a rock,
Or a towering mountain, lofty and high.

Based on what has been established, the estimate of the omitted part is not what al-Zamakhshari said. Rather the estimate is: had our Lord willed the sending down of angels with the message from Him to mankind, He would have sent them down to them with it. This is more emphatic in refusing the sending of a human being, since they made that dependent on the words of the angels, while He did not will that. So how would He will it in a human being?

﴿فَإنّا بِما أُرْسِلْتُمْ بِهِ كافِرُونَ﴾: an address to Hud, Salih, and whoever of the prophets called to faith; the address was given precedence over the third person, as in your saying: "You and Zayd will stand" (anta wa-Zayd taqūmān).

(Mā) is verbal-noun (maṣdariyya), meaning: with your sending, and (bihi) is an emphasis for that. It may also be that (mā) means (alladhī), and the pronoun in (bihi) refers back to it; when they disbelieve in what the sending contains, that is disbelief in the sending.

Their words ﴿بِما أُرْسِلْتُمْ﴾ are not an acknowledgment of the sending, but are in the manner of mockery, meaning: with what you were sent, according to your claim, just as Pharaoh said: ﴿إنَّ رَسُولَكُمُ الَّذِي أُرْسِلَ إلَيْكم لَمَجْنُونٌ﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 27].

When He, exalted is He, had explained the disbelief of ʿAd and Thamud in general terms, He then detailed it, mentioning the distinctive feature of each of the two groups.

He said: ﴿فَأمّا عادٌ فاسْتَكْبَرُوا﴾, meaning: they magnified themselves against obeying God's command and against what the messengers brought them. ﴿بِغَيْرِ الحَقِّ﴾ means: without what they deserved.

When He mentioned to them this great sin, which is arrogance, and since it was an inward act, He mentioned what appeared upon them of the outward act that expresses what is in the heart: ﴿وقالُوا مَن أشَدُّ مِنّا قُوَّةً﴾, meaning: no one is stronger than us, because of what God had given them of great physical stature and severity of force. God answered them by saying that the One who gave them that is stronger than them in strength. And although they knew God's signs, they used to deny them and not acknowledge them, just as the depositary denies the deposit to its owner while knowing it.

The word (kāna) in much usage indicates continuity. He expressed power by strength (quwwa), so just as one says "God is more capable than them" (Allahu aqdaru minhum), one also says "God is stronger than them" (Allahu aqwā minhum). The two kinds of power share a common measure, even though each of the two powers has its own distinct characteristic, just as God is described with knowledge and a human being is described with knowledge.

Then He mentioned what befell ʿAd through it, saying: ﴿فَأرْسَلْنا عَلَيْهِمْ رِيحًا صَرْصَرًا﴾. In a hadith: "God commanded the keepers of the wind, and they opened it upon them to the size of a ring's hole. Had they opened it to the size of a bull's nostril, the world would have been destroyed."

It is also related that it used to carry the caravan with its loads and throw them into the sea.

As for ṣarṣar, Mujahid said: it means intensely hot with poisonous blasts. Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Dahhak, Qatadah and al-Sudi said: it derives from ṣirr, i.e., cold.

al-Sudi also said, as did Abu ʿUbayda, Ibn Qutaybah, al-Tabari, and a group: it derives from ṣarṣara, when it made a sound.

Ibn al-Sikkit said: ṣarṣar may be from ṣarra, which is a cry, and from it comes: ﴿فَأقْبَلَتِ امْرَأتُهُ في صَرَّةٍ﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 29]. Ṣarṣar is also a river in Iraq.

The two Haramis (Ibn Kathir and Nafiʿ? as the common reading of the two Meccan and Medinan readers), Abu ʿAmr, al-Nakhaʿi, ʿIsa, and al-Aʿraj read (nahsātin) with a sukun on the ḥāʾ. This may be a verbal noun described by it, and sometimes it is made its annexed noun; it may also be a lightened form of faʿʿala. al-Tabari said: naḥusa and naḥisa mean: he hated.

al-Zamakhshari said: it is a lightened form of naḥḥasa, or an adjective of the pattern faʿʿala, or a description by a verbal noun. End of his words.

I investigated what the morphologists mentioned of adjectives from the intransitive faʿala pattern, and they did not mention any verb with a sukun on the ʿayn. They said: it comes in the pattern faʿila, like fariḥa, and he is fariḥ; and in the pattern afʿala, like ḥawara, and he is aḥwar; and in the pattern faʿlān, like shabiʿa, and he is shabʿān; and it may come in the pattern fāʿil, like salima, and he is sālim, and balliya, and he is bāl.

Qatadah, Abu Raja', al-Jahdari, [p. 491] Shayba, Abu Jaʿfar, al-Aʿmash, and the rest of the Seven read with a kasra on the ḥāʾ, which is the analogical form. The ṣaʿqah is the single occurrence: one says ṣaʿaqathu al-ṣāʿiqah fa-ṣuʿiqa (the thunderbolt struck him so he was struck down), and it is of the pattern faʿala with a fatha on the ʿayn, so the passive is fuʿila with a kasra, like khadaʿathu fa-khudiʿa (he deceived him so he was deceived). (Idh) is governed by (ṣāʿiqatan), because its meaning is punishment.

﴿مِن بَيْنِ أيْدِيهِمْ ومِن خَلْفِهِمْ﴾: Ibn ʿAbbas said: i.e., before them and after them, that is, before Hud and Salih and after them both.

It was also said: [it refers to] those who were sent to their forefathers and those who were sent to them. So ﴿مِن بَيْنِ أيْدِيهِمْ﴾ means: from before them, and ﴿ومِن خَلْفِهِمْ﴾ means: the messengers who were present with them. Thus the pronoun in (min khalfihim) refers to the messengers. This was said by al-Dahhak, and al-Farra' followed him, and a similar view will come from al-Tabari.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: ﴿مِن بَيْنِ أيْدِيهِمْ﴾ means: they preceded in time, and their warning was connected to the lifetimes of ʿAd and Thamud, and by this connection the proof was established.

﴿ومِن خَلْفِهِمْ﴾ means: a messenger came to them after their existence in time had passed. From the whole expression comes the establishment of proof against them, in that the message and the warning reached them both through report and through direct encounter. End of his words, and this is an explanation of Ibn ʿAbbas's statement.

al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿مِن بَيْنِ أيْدِيهِمْ ومِن خَلْفِهِمْ﴾ means: they came to them from every side, exerted themselves with them, and applied every stratagem with them, yet they found from them only obstinacy and aversion, as God related about Satan: ﴿لَآتِيَنَّهم مِن بَيْنِ أيْدِيهِمْ ومِن خَلْفِهِمْ وعَنْ أيْمانِهِمْ وعَنْ شَمائِلِهِمْ﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 17], meaning: I will come to them from every direction, and I will apply every stratagem against them.

It is reported from al-Hasan: they warned them of God's deeds regarding the nations before them and of the punishment of the Hereafter; for when they warned them of that, they had brought them admonition from the direction of the past time and what occurred in it upon the disbelievers, and from the direction of the future and what would befall them. End of his words.

al-Tabari said: the pronoun in His saying ﴿ومِن خَلْفِهِمْ﴾ refers to the messengers, and in ﴿مِن بَيْنِ أيْدِيهِمْ﴾ it refers to the nations. This departs from the apparent sense by separating the pronouns and obscuring the meaning, for the sense would become: the messengers came to them from before them and came to them from behind the messengers, that is, from behind themselves. This meaning is not intelligible unless the pronoun in (khalfihim) refers to (al-rusul) verbally, while it refers to other messengers in meaning. So it is as if He said: the messengers came to them from before them and from behind other messengers. This is like their saying: "I have a dirham and half of it," meaning: and half of another dirham. This is far-fetched.

From among the destroyed nations, ʿAd and Thamud were singled out for mention because the Quraysh knew their situation, and because they had settled upon their lands, in Yemen and al-Hijr. al-Afwah al-Awdi said:

They became like Qil ibn ʿAnz among his tribe, when ʿAd was destroyed by that which it had done.
Or after him like Qudar, when peoples followed him in error; so they perished.

(An lā taʿbudū) may be an explanatory (an), because the coming of the messengers to them implies the sense of speech, meaning: they came to them addressing them. It may also be a lightened form of the heavy (anna), meaning: that do not worship, the governing particle being for the imperfect verb, and it is joined to the prohibition just as it is joined to illa, as in ﴿أنْ طَهِّرا﴾ [al-Baqarah: 125], and as in "I wrote to him with an qum" (that stand up). In this construction there is only the sense of prohibition. It is also permissible, though far-fetched, for (lā) to be a negation and (an) to be a governing particle for the verb; this was said by al-Hawfi, and he mentioned no other view. The object of (shāʾa) is omitted, and al-Zamakhshari estimated it as: had our Lord willed [p. 490] the sending of messengers, He would have sent down angels. End of his words.

I investigated what has come in the Qur'an and in Arabic speech of this construction, and I found that the omitted part is never anything other than the same as the answer, such as His saying: ﴿ولَوْ شاءَ اللَّهُ لَجَمَعَهم عَلى الهُدى﴾ [al-Anʿam: 35], meaning: had God willed to gather them upon guidance, He would have gathered them upon it. Similarly: ﴿لَوْ نَشاءُ لَجَعَلْناهُ حُطامًا﴾ [al-Waqiʿah: 65], ﴿لَوْ نَشاءُ جَعَلْناهُ أُجاجًا﴾ [al-Waqiʿah: 70], ﴿ولَوْ شاءَ رَبُّكَ لَآمَنَ﴾ [Yunus: 99], ﴿ولَوْ شاءَ رَبُّكَ ما فَعَلُوهُ﴾ [al-Anʿam: 112], ﴿لَوْ شاءَ اللَّهُ ما عَبَدْنا مِن دُونِهِ مِن شَيْءٍ﴾ [al-Nahl: 35]. The poet said:

Had my Lord willed, I would have been Qays ibn Khalid,
And had my Lord willed, I would have been ʿUmar ibn Marthad.

The rajaz poet said:

And one who, had he willed, would have been a rock,
Or a towering mountain, lofty and high.

Based on what has been established, the estimate of the omitted part is not what al-Zamakhshari said. Rather the estimate is: had our Lord willed the sending down of angels with the message from Him to mankind, He would have sent them down to them with it. This is more emphatic in refusing the sending of a human being, since they made that dependent on the words of the angels, while He did not will that. So how would He will it in a human being?

﴿فَإنّا بِما أُرْسِلْتُمْ بِهِ كافِرُونَ﴾: an address to Hud, Salih, and whoever of the prophets called to faith; the address was given precedence over the third person, as in your saying: "You and Zayd will stand" (anta wa-Zayd taqūmān).

(Mā) is verbal-noun (maṣdariyya), meaning: with your sending, and (bihi) is an emphasis for that. It may also be that (mā) means (alladhī), and the pronoun in (bihi) refers back to it; when they disbelieve in what the sending contains, that is disbelief in the sending.

Their words ﴿بِما أُرْسِلْتُمْ﴾ are not an acknowledgment of the sending, but are in the manner of mockery, meaning: with what you were sent, according to your claim, just as Pharaoh said: ﴿إنَّ رَسُولَكُمُ الَّذِي أُرْسِلَ إلَيْكم لَمَجْنُونٌ﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 27].

When He, exalted is He, had explained the disbelief of ʿAd and Thamud in general terms, He then detailed it, mentioning the distinctive feature of each of the two groups.

He said: ﴿فَأمّا عادٌ فاسْتَكْبَرُوا﴾, meaning: they magnified themselves against obeying God's command and against what the messengers brought them. ﴿بِغَيْرِ الحَقِّ﴾ means: without what they deserved.

When He mentioned to them this great sin, which is arrogance, and since it was an inward act, He mentioned what appeared upon them of the outward act that expresses what is in the heart: ﴿وقالُوا مَن أشَدُّ مِنّا قُوَّةً﴾, meaning: no one is stronger than us, because of what God had given them of great physical stature and severity of force. God answered them by saying that the One who gave them that is stronger than them in strength. And although they knew God's signs, they used to deny them and not acknowledge them, just as the depositary denies the deposit to its owner while knowing it.

The word (kāna) in much usage indicates continuity. He expressed power by strength (quwwa), so just as one says "God is more capable than them" (Allahu aqdaru minhum), one also says "God is stronger than them" (Allahu aqwā minhum). The two kinds of power share a common measure, even though each of the two powers has its own distinct characteristic, just as God is described with knowledge and a human being is described with knowledge.

Then He mentioned what befell ʿAd through it, saying: ﴿فَأرْسَلْنا عَلَيْهِمْ رِيحًا صَرْصَرًا﴾. In a hadith: "God commanded the keepers of the wind, and they opened it upon them to the size of a ring's hole. Had they opened it to the size of a bull's nostril, the world would have been destroyed."

It is also related that it used to carry the caravan with its loads and throw them into the sea.

As for ṣarṣar, Mujahid said: it means intensely hot with poisonous blasts. Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Dahhak, Qatadah and al-Sudi said: it derives from ṣirr, i.e., cold.

al-Sudi also said, as did Abu ʿUbayda, Ibn Qutaybah, al-Tabari, and a group: it derives from ṣarṣara, when it made a sound.

Ibn al-Sikkit said: ṣarṣar may be from ṣarra, which is a cry, and from it comes: ﴿فَأقْبَلَتِ امْرَأتُهُ في صَرَّةٍ﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 29]. Ṣarṣar is also a river in Iraq.

The two Haramis (Ibn Kathir and Nafiʿ? as the common reading of the two Meccan and Medinan readers), Abu ʿAmr, al-Nakhaʿi, ʿIsa, and al-Aʿraj read (nahsātin) with a sukun on the ḥāʾ. This may be a verbal noun described by it, and sometimes it is made its annexed noun; it may also be a lightened form of faʿʿala. al-Tabari said: naḥusa and naḥisa mean: he hated.

al-Zamakhshari said: it is a lightened form of naḥḥasa, or an adjective of the pattern faʿʿala, or a description by a verbal noun. End of his words.

I investigated what the morphologists mentioned of adjectives from the intransitive faʿala pattern, and they did not mention any verb with a sukun on the ʿayn. They said: it comes in the pattern faʿila, like fariḥa, and he is fariḥ; and in the pattern afʿala, like ḥawara, and he is aḥwar; and in the pattern faʿlān, like shabiʿa, and he is shabʿān; and it may come in the pattern fāʿil, like salima, and he is sālim, and balliya, and he is bāl.

Qatadah, Abu Raja', al-Jahdari, [p. 491] Shayba, Abu Jaʿfar, al-Aʿmash, and the rest of the Seven read with a kasra on the ḥāʾ, which is the analogical form. Its verb is naḥisa on the pattern faʿila with a kasra on the ʿayn. ﴿نَحِساتٍ﴾ is an adjective of (ayyām), pluralized with alif and tāʾ, because it is the plural of an adjective for something non-rational.

Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Sudi said: ill-omened, from the well-known ill omen (naḥs). al-Dahhak said: intensely cold, to the point that the cold became a punishment for them. al-Asmaʿi recited, using naḥs in the sense of cold:

As if a clear wine had appeared with naḥs,
Whose dew made the pure water appear.

It was also said: it was named so because it was full of dust, and from this is the rajaz poet's saying:

I set out before the rising of the sun
To hunt on a day of little naḥs.

He means: little dust.

Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and Qatadah said: they were consecutive days, from the last Wednesday of Shawwal to the next Wednesday.

al-Sudi said: the first of them was the morning of Sunday. al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas said: Friday. Yahya ibn Salam said: Sunday.

﴿لِنُذِيقَهم عَذابَ الخِزْيِ في الحَياةِ الدُّنْيا﴾: this is destruction. It was also read (litudhīqahum) with a tāʾ. al-Zamakhshari said: [the subject is] the wind, or the ill-omened days. He attributed the punishment to disgrace as the attribution of a qualified noun to its qualifier, not using another word that implies sharing and detail. As for the statement about ﴿ولَعَذابُ الآخِرَةِ﴾, it is a figurative attribution, or the description of the punishment as disgraceful is more emphatic than describing them with it. Do you not see the difference between your saying "he is a poet" and "he has the poetry of a poet"? He matched their arrogance with the punishment of disgrace, which is humiliation and abasement.

He began with the story of ʿAd because it is older in time, then mentioned Thamud, saying: ﴿وأمّا ثَمُودُ﴾. The majority read it in the nominative as diptote (mamnūʿ min al-ṣarf). Ibn Wathhab, al-Aʿmash, and Bakr ibn Habib read it as declinable (maṣrūfan). This is the reading of Ibn Wathhab and al-Aʿmash for (Thamūd) with tanwin throughout the Qur'an, except His saying ﴿وآتَيْنا ثَمُودَ النّاقَةَ﴾ [al-Isra: 59], because in the codex it is written without an alif. It was also read as (Thamūda) in the accusative, diptote, and al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, and al-Aʿmash read (Thamūdan) in the accusative with tanwin. al-Mufaddal related from ʿAsim both readings. End of his words.

﴿فَهَدَيْناهُمْ﴾: Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatadah, al-Sudi and Ibn Zayd said: We made clear to them.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: guidance here does not mean direction (irshad). al-Farra', followed by al-Zamakhshari, said: ﴿فَهَدَيْناهُمْ﴾ means: We showed them the path of error and of right guidance, as in His saying: ﴿وهَدَيْناهُ النَّجْدَيْنِ﴾ [al-Balad: 10].

﴿فاسْتَحَبُّوا العَمى عَلى الهُدى﴾: they chose entry into error over entry into right guidance.

(If you say:) Does not the meaning of "hadaytuhu" (I guided him) denote that guidance came to be in him, the evidence for which is your saying "hadaytuhu fa-htada" (I guided him, so he was guided), in the sense of attaining and achieving the desired goal, just as you say "radda'tuhu fa-rtada'a" (I deterred him, so he was deterred)? How, then, is it permissible to use it for mere indication (al-dalalah al-mujarradah)?

(I say:) It is for indicating that He enabled them and removed their excuses, so that they had no pretext or cause left. Thus it is as if He attained the desired end in them by bringing about what necessitates and entails it. End of quote. And this is according to the方法 of the Mu'tazilah.

Sufyan said: "da'awnahum" (we called them). Ibn Zayd said: "a'lamnahumu al-huda min al-dalal" (we made them know guidance from misguidance).

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "fa-istahabbu" is an expression for their acquiring blindness (by their own earning), otherwise it is by Allah's origination. And what indicates that it refers to their acquisition is His saying: "bi-ma kanu yaksibun" (for what they used to earn). End of quote.

Al-Hun: humiliation (al-hawan). The punishment is described by the verbal noun, or it is a substitute for it. Ibn Miqsam recited: "'adhab al-hawan" with a fatha on the ha' and an alif after the waw.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Even if there were in the Qur'an no proof against the Qadariyyah, who are the Magians of this Ummah, by the testimony of its Prophet, and he is sufficient as a witness, except this (verse), it would suffice as a proof." End of quote, in keeping with his habit of reviling the People of the Sunnah.

Then He reminded Quraysh of the salvation of those who believed and were God-fearing. It was said: among those who responded and were saved from the believers were Hud and Salih, and one hundred and ten persons.

[p. 489]

﴿But if they turn away, say: "I have warned you of a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of ʿAd and Thamud."﴾ ﴿When the messengers came to them from before them and from behind them, saying, "Worship none but God." They said, "Had our Lord willed, He would have sent down angels. So we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent."﴾ ﴿As for ʿAd, they were arrogant on earth without right and said, "Who is stronger than us in strength?" Did they not see that God, who created them, is stronger than them in strength? And they used to deny Our signs.﴾ ﴿So We sent upon them a furious wind during ill-omened days, that We might make them taste the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world. But the punishment of the Hereafter is more disgracing, and they will not be helped.﴾ ﴿As for Thamud, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance, so the thunderbolt of the humiliating punishment seized them for what they used to earn.﴾ ﴿And We saved those who believed and used to be God-fearing.﴾

﴿فَإنْ أعْرَضُوا﴾: a shift (iltifat) from the second-person address in His saying ﴿أئِنَّكم لَتَكْفُرُونَ﴾ [Fussilat: 9] to the third-person pronoun, as a turning away from addressing them, since they had already been reminded, with the proofs that call for their attention and faith, of the Oneness and the overwhelming power. ﴿فَقُلْ أنْذَرْتُكُمْ﴾ means: I have informed you. (ṣāʿiqatan) means: the descent of a thunderbolt. Qatadah said: a punishment like the punishment of ʿAd and Thamud.

al-Zamakhshari said: a punishment of severe impact, as if it were a thunderbolt.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿صاعِقَةً مِثْلَ صاعِقَةِ﴾, while Ibn al-Zubayr, al-Sulami, al-Nakhaʿi and Ibn Muhaysin read them without the alif in both places and with a sukun on the ʿayn. Its explanation has already been given at the beginning of al-Baqarah.

(Idh) is governed by (ṣāʿiqatan), because its meaning is punishment.

﴿مِن بَيْنِ أيْدِيهِمْ ومِن خَلْفِهِمْ﴾: Ibn ʿAbbas said: i.e., before them and after them, that is, before Hud and Salih and after them both.

It was also said: [it refers to] those who were sent to their forefathers and those who were sent to them. So ﴿مِن بَيْنِ أيْدِيهِمْ﴾ means: from before them, and ﴿ومِن خَلْفِهِمْ﴾ means: the messengers who were present with them. Thus the pronoun in (min khalfihim) refers to the messengers. ﴿ومِن خَلْفِهِمْ﴾ means: a messenger came to them after their existence in time had passed. From the whole expression comes the establishment of proof against them, in that the message and the warning reached them both through report and through direct encounter. End of his words, and this is an explanation of Ibn ʿAbbas's statement.

al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿مِن بَيْنِ أيْدِيهِمْ ومِن خَلْفِهِمْ﴾ means: they came to them from every side, exerted themselves with them, and applied every stratagem with them, yet they found from them only obstinacy and aversion, as God related about Satan: ﴿لَآتِيَنَّهم مِن بَيْنِ أيْدِيهِمْ ومِن خَلْفِهِمْ وعَنْ أيْمانِهِمْ وعَنْ شَمائِلِهِمْ﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 17], meaning: I will come to them from every direction, and I will apply every stratagem against them.

It is reported from al-Hasan: they warned them of God's deeds regarding the nations before them and of the punishment of the Hereafter; for when they warned them of that, they had brought them admonition from the direction of the past time and what occurred in it upon the disbelievers, and from the direction of the future and what would befall them. End of his words.

al-Tabari said: the pronoun in His saying ﴿ومِن خَلْفِهِمْ﴾ refers to the messengers, and in ﴿مِن بَيْنِ أيْدِيهِمْ﴾ it refers to the nations. This departs from the apparent sense by separating the pronouns and obscuring the meaning, for the sense would become: the messengers came to them from before them and came to them from behind the messengers, that is, from behind themselves. This meaning is not intelligible unless the pronoun in (khalfihim) refers to (al-rusul) verbally, while it refers to other messengers in meaning. So it is as if He said: the messengers came to them from before them and from behind other messengers. This is like their saying: "I have a dirham and half of it," meaning: and half of another dirham. This is far-fetched.

They became like Qil ibn ʿAnz among his tribe, when ʿAd was destroyed by that which it had done.
Or after him like Qudar, when peoples followed him in error; so they perished.

Similarly: ﴿لَوْ نَشاءُ لَجَعَلْناهُ حُطامًا﴾ [al-Waqiʿah: 65], ﴿لَوْ نَشاءُ جَعَلْناهُ أُجاجًا﴾ [al-Waqiʿah: 70], ﴿ولَوْ شاءَ رَبُّكَ لَآمَنَ﴾ [Yunus: 99], ﴿ولَوْ شاءَ رَبُّكَ ما فَعَلُوهُ﴾ [al-Anʿam: 112], ﴿لَوْ شاءَ اللَّهُ ما عَبَدْنا مِن دُونِهِ مِن شَيْءٍ﴾ [al-Nahl: 35]. The poet said:

Had my Lord willed, I would have been Qays ibn Khalid,
And had my Lord willed, I would have been ʿUmar ibn Marthad.

And one who, had he willed, would have been a rock,
Or a towering mountain, lofty and high.
