﴿A recompense for what they used to deny Our signs﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: their recompense is for what they used to engage in idle talk about in it, so he mentioned denial, which is the cause of the idle talk. When the disbelievers saw the magnitude of the punishment of the Fire that had befallen them, they asked God, exalted is He, to show them the one who had been the cause of their misguidance and leading astray. The apparent meaning is that "those who" (alladhayn) is intended as a genus, i.e., every misleader of these two kinds. It is reported from ʿAli and Qatada that they are Iblis and Qabil: Iblis instituted disbelief, and Qabil instituted killing without right.

It was said: Is this statement from ʿAli sound? Qabil was a believing sinner, and they only sought those who misled them into disbelief, which leads to eternity. This statement has been reconciled by saying: Qabil sought every sinner among the people of major sins, and Iblis sought every disbeliever. The wording of the verse rejects this statement and its reconciliation. The disagreement over the reading of (arina) in His saying: ﴿And show us our rites﴾ [al-Baqarah: 128] has already been mentioned.

Al-Zamakhshari said: They related from al-Khalil that if you say arini thawbaka with a kasra, the meaning is "let me see it," and if you say it with sukun, it is a request for gifts, meaning "give me your garment." Its parallel is the common use of ityaʾ in the sense of iʿtaʾ, whose original meaning is "bringing." End.

﴿We will put them beneath our feet﴾: they mean at the lowest level of the Fire, which is more severe in punishment, and it is the abode of the hypocrites.

The doubling of the nun in alladhayni, allatayni, hadhayni and hatayni when they are in the oblique case with ya' is not permitted by the Basrians, and the reading with it in the seven readers is a proof against them.

[p. 492] ﴿On the Day when the enemies of Allah are gathered to the Fire, they will be marshalled in ranks.﴾ ﴿Until, when they reach it, their hearing, their sight and their skins will testify against them concerning what they used to do.﴾ ﴿They will say to their skins, "Why did you testify against us?" They will say, "Allah has caused us to speak, He who causes everything to speak. He created you the first time, and to Him you are returned."﴾ ﴿You did not conceal yourselves so that your hearing, your sight and your skins would not testify against you, but you thought that Allah does not know much of what you do.﴾ ﴿That was your assumption which you assumed about your Lord; it has destroyed you, and you have become among the losers.﴾ ﴿If they endure, the Fire is their abode; and if they seek to be pleased, they will not be among those who are granted that.﴾ ﴿We appointed for them companions who made attractive to them what was before them and what was behind them, and the word has become due against them, among nations that passed away before them, of jinn and humankind. Indeed, they were losers.﴾ ﴿Those who disbelieved said, "Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it, that you may overcome."﴾ ﴿So We will surely make those who disbelieved taste a severe punishment, and We will surely recompense them with the worst of what they used to do.﴾ ﴿That is the recompense of the enemies of Allah: the Fire; for them therein is the abode of eternity, as a recompense for what they used to deny of Our signs.﴾ ﴿Those who disbelieved will say, "Our Lord, show us the two who led us astray, of the jinn and humankind, that we may put them under our feet so that they will be among the lowest."﴾

When Allah, the Exalted, explained the manner of the punishment of those disbelievers in this world, He followed it with the manner of the punishment of those disbelievers and others. The word "the Day" (yawma) is governed by ﴿remember﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 110). The majority of readers recited "yuhsharu" in the passive voice with "a'da'" in the nominative, but Zayd ibn 'Ali, Nafi', al-A'raj and the people of Madinah read it with the nun (nuhshiru), with "a'da'" in the accusative; al-A'raj also vowelled the shin with a kasra.

The meaning of "yuza'un" (they will be marshalled in ranks) has been mentioned in Surah al-Naml, and "until" (hatta) marks the endpoint of ﴿they are gathered﴾ (al-An'am: 51). "The enemies of Allah" are the disbelievers of the earlier and later generations. The "ma" after "idha" is extra, for emphasis.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning of emphasis in it is that the time of their coming to the Fire is necessarily the time of testimony against them, and there is no way for it to be free of that. A similar example is His saying: ﴿Is it then, when it has occurred, that you will believe in it?﴾ (Yunus: 51), meaning: the time of its occurrence must be the time of their belief in it. End of quote.

I do not understand how the addition of "ma" after "idha" conveys emphasis. Had the construction been without "ma", the fulfilment of the condition would undoubtedly occur without delay, since the conditional particle is an adverb of time, so the testimony would certainly take place at that time. In the speech there is an omission; the implied sense is: ﴿until, when they reach it﴾, that is, the Fire, and they are questioned about what they committed, and they deny it, ﴿their hearing, their sight and their skins will testify against them﴾ concerning the crimes they earned. They had supposed that there was no witness against them.

There is a hadith: "The first part of a person to speak will be his left thigh, then the limbs will speak, and he will say: 'Woe to you! It was for you that I was defending myself.'"

The senses are five: hearing, sight, smell, taste and touch. Since taste is included within touch, for through the contact of the skin of the tongue and palate with the food the tasting is perceived, and since the goodness of smell involves no obligation, no command and no prohibition, and it is weak, he limited the senses to hearing, sight and touch, since these are the ones in which obligation has come. He did not mention the sense of smell because there is no obligation in it. So this, and Allah knows best, is the wisdom of limiting it to these three.

The apparent meaning is that "skins" (julud) refers to the well-known skins. It is also said that it refers to the limbs, and that it is a metonymy for them. It is also said that it is a metonymy for the private parts. It has been said that most of the commentators hold this view, among them Ibn 'Abbas, just as marriage is referred to metaphorically as "secret" [p. 493].

﴿For what they used to do﴾ of crimes.

Then they questioned their skins about the reason for their testimony against them, and the skins did not mention any reason except that Allah, the Exalted, had caused them to speak.

Since from them there proceeded what proceeds from rational beings, namely testimony, they addressed them with the words: ﴿Why did you testify against us?﴾, addressing them as they would address rational beings.

Zayd ibn 'Ali read: "lima shahidtunna" (why did you testify, feminine plural), using the feminine pronoun. "Kulla shay'" (everything) is not meant in its full generality; rather the meaning is: every speaker to whom speech is customary, or in whom that would be a breach of custom.

Al-Zamakhshari said: By "kulla shay'" he meant every animal, just as he meant by it in His saying: ﴿Allah is capable of everything﴾ (al-Baqarah: 284), i.e., of things within the scope of power. The meaning is that our speaking is no wonder from the power of Allah, who has power to cause every animal to speak, and to create you and bring you into being, and to restore you and return you to His recompense. They only said to them ﴿Why did you testify against us?﴾ because they were overwhelmed by their testimony and it was too grievous for them to be exposed by the tongues of their limbs.

Al-Zamakhshari also said: If you ask: how can their sight testify against them, and how can it speak? I say: Allah, Exalted and Mighty, causes it to speak, just as He caused the tree to speak by creating speech in it. End of quote. This man is attached to his Mu'tazili doctrine (a rationalist school of theology), and he brings it into everything he can.

By his saying "just as He caused the tree to speak by creating speech in it," he indicated that Allah did not literally speak to Musa; rather it was the tree from which he heard the speech, Allah having created speech in it, and the tree addressed him with it on behalf of Allah, the Exalted.

The apparent meaning is that His saying ﴿You did not conceal yourselves﴾ is part of the speech of the limbs. It has been said that it may also be part of the speech of Allah, the Exalted, rebuking them, or part of the speech of an angel commanded by Him. As for ﴿that your hearing would testify against you﴾ (an yashhada): it may mean: out of fear, or for fear that it would testify, if you were not aware that it would testify. ﴿But you thought that Allah does not know﴾: so you became absorbed and persisted. Mujahid took this view. Concealment (al-sitr) also comes in this sense, as the poet said:

"Concealment is before the immoral deeds, and what meets you before goodness is a concealment."

It may also mean: "from" that it would testify, i.e., you did not refrain, and it was not possible for you to hide from your limbs or conceal yourselves from them by your disbelief and your sins; nor did you think that they would reach this degree of testimony against you.

Al-Suddi took this view. Or it may mean: you did not expect, by hiding and concealing, that it would testify against you, because the limbs are constantly with you.

Qatadah expressed ﴿you conceal yourselves﴾ by "you thought," i.e., you did not think that it would testify. This is an explanation in meaning, not a synonym of the wording. ﴿But you thought that Allah does not know much﴾, meaning the hidden things of your deeds. This assumption is disbelief and ignorance of Allah and a corrupt belief which leads to denying the messengers and doubting the knowledge of God.

﴿That﴾ refers to their assumption that Allah does not know much of their deeds. It is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿has destroyed you﴾; and ﴿your assumption﴾ is an apposition to ﴿that﴾: i.e., your assumption about your Lord, that is what destroyed you.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿Your assumption﴾ and ﴿has destroyed you﴾ are two predicates. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: ﴿has destroyed you﴾ may be a predicate after a predicate. End of quote.

It is not valid for ﴿your assumption about your Lord﴾ to be a predicate, because His saying ﴿that﴾ refers to their earlier assumption, so the meaning would become: your assumption that your Lord does not know is your assumption about your Lord; thus what is conveyed by the predicate would be what is conveyed by the subject, which is impermissible. This is like the example the grammarians prohibited: "the master of the slave-girl is her owner."

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The Kufans permitted the meaning of ﴿has destroyed you﴾ to be in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), whereas the Basrans do not permit a past verb to be a circumstantial clause unless it is accompanied by "qad," and it may be possible to assume "qad" according to them if it does not appear. End of quote.

Al-Akhfash, from the Basrans, permitted a past verb to be a circumstantial clause without assuming "qad," and this is the correct view, since this usage is so frequent in the language of the Arabs as to necessitate analogy, and interpretation becomes far-fetched. We have mentioned the abundance of evidence for this in our book called "al-Tadhyil wal-Takmil fi Sharh al-Tashil."

﴿If they endure﴾: the address is to the Prophet, peace be upon him. It has been said that there is an omission in the speech, its implied meaning being: "whether they endure or do not endure," as in His saying: ﴿So endure or do not endure, it is the same for you﴾ (al-Tur: 16), and that is on the Day of Resurrection.

It has been said that the implied meaning is: if they endure in abandoning your religion and following their desires, ﴿the Fire is their abode﴾, i.e., the place of dwelling.

The majority read ﴿if they seek to be pleased﴾ (yastatibu) in the active voice, and ﴿they will not be among those who are granted that﴾ (al-mu'tabin), with the active participle. Al-Dahhak said: If they make excuses, they will not be among those who are excused.

It has also been said: even if they seek the pleasure (al-'utba), which is contentment, they are not among those who are given it and deserve it.

Al-Hasan, 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd and Musa al-Aswari read ﴿if they are sought to be pleased﴾ (yustatabu) in the passive voice, and ﴿among those who are granted that﴾ (al-mu'tabin) as an active participle, meaning: they were asked to please their Lord, but they will not do so; and this will not happen, because they have departed the world, the abode of deeds.

As it was said: "There is no seeking of pleasure after death." Abu Dhu'ayb said:

"Do you grieve for death and its doubts? / Time does not grant pleasure to one who despairs."

It may also be that this reading means: even if they were returned, they would go back to what they were forbidden.

When Allah, the Exalted, mentioned the severe threat in this world and the Hereafter upon the disbelief of those disbelievers, He followed it with mention of the cause that brought them into disbelief, saying: ﴿We appointed for them companions﴾, i.e., We caused them to be, from a direction they did not expect.

It has also been said: We empowered and entrusted them over them. It has also been said: We decreed for them. And "qurana'" is the plural of "qarin" (companion), i.e., evil companions from among the misguided jinn and humankind; ﴿so they made attractive to them﴾, i.e., they beautified and embellished in their own souls; ﴿what was before them﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: from the matters of the Hereafter, that there is no Paradise, no Fire and no resurrection.

﴿And what was behind them﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: from the matters of this world, from error and disbelief and the pleasures of this world. Al-Kalbi said: ﴿What was before them﴾ is their deeds which they witness, and ﴿what was behind them﴾ is what they will do in the future.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: ﴿What was before them﴾ is their bad beliefs about the messengers and prophethood, praise of idol worship, and following the practice of the fathers; ﴿what was behind them﴾ is what comes after them of the matters of the Resurrection and the return. End of quote, in summary; this is an explanation of al-Hasan's view, who said: ﴿what was before them﴾ is from the matters of this world, and ﴿what was behind them﴾ is from the matters of the Hereafter.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, how could He appoint for them companions from the devils, when He forbids them from following their footsteps? I say: its meaning is that He abandoned them and withheld success from them because of their determination in disbelief, so no companions remained for them except the devils. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿And whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful, We appoint for him a devil﴾ (al-Zukhruf: 36). End of quote, and this is in the manner of the Mu'tazila.

﴿And the word has become due against them﴾, i.e., the word of punishment, which is the decree that is binding, that they are to be punished.

﴿Among nations﴾, i.e., among a number of nations. On this basis is the poet's saying:

"If you are, from the best of conduct, one who is turned away, / then among others too have been led astray."

That is: you are among a number of others, or among the count of others; in this you are not unique.

It has also been said: "fi" (among) means "ma'a" (with), though there is no need for such implication since the meaning of "fi" is correct. The position of ﴿among nations﴾ is accusative as a circumstantial clause, i.e., being among a number of nations, and the one qualified is the pronoun in ﴿against them﴾.

﴿Indeed, they were losers﴾: the pronoun refers to them and to the nations, and this is the reason for their deserving the punishment.

﴿Those who disbelieved said: Do not listen﴾, i.e., do not give ear, ﴿to this Qur'an, and make noise during it﴾: when Muhammad ﷺ recites it.

Abu al-'Aliyah said: Fall into it and find fault with it. Others said: When the Messenger, peace be upon him, recited in the mosque, people, believers and disbelievers alike, would listen to him. The disbelievers feared that the hearts would be won over by that, so they said: Whenever Muhammad ﷺ recites, let us make noise with whistling, clapping and shouting, reciting poetry and rhymed prose, until his voice is hidden. This act is the "laghw" (idle noise).

Al-Jumhur and al-Farra' read it with a fath on the ghayn, the present of "laghiya" with a kasra; Bakr ibn Habib al-Sahmi is also reported thus in the book of Ibn 'Atiyyah, and in the book "al-Lawamih."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 41, verse 19–29 (part 2 of 2):

As for the book of Ibn Khalawayh, ʿAbd Allah ibn Bakr al-Sahmi, Qatada, Abu Haywa, al-Zaʿfarani, Ibn Abi Ishaq and ʿIsa (report it) with a variant from them: with a damma on the ghayn, as the present tense of laghā (with a fatha), and both are dialects, meaning: "Introduce into it idle talk (laghw)," which is the varying of speech with what has no benefit in it.

Al-Akhfash said: it is said laghā yalghā with a fatha on the ghayn, though its analogical form is with a damma, but it was given a fatha because of a guttural letter. So the first reading is from yalghī, and the second is from yalghū.

The author of al-Lawami said: it is also possible that the fatha is from laghā bi-l-shayʾ, yalghā bihi, when one throws it, so that fīhi (in it) means bihi (with it), i.e., "Throw it and cast it away."

﴿Perhaps you will overcome﴾: that is, you will obliterate its matter and extinguish its remembrance.

﴿Then We will surely make those who disbelieved taste﴾: a severe threat to the Quraysh. The severe punishment in this world is like the battle of Badr and others, and the worst is on the Day of Resurrection.

God, exalted is He, swore on both sentences, and "those who disbelieved" includes the speakers and the addressees in His saying: ﴿And those who disbelieved said, "Do not listen to this Qur'an"﴾.

﴿That﴾, i.e., their recompense in the Hereafter: "the Fire" is either a substitute (badal) or the predicate of an omitted subject. It is also permitted that "that" is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "the matter is that," and "recompense" (jazaʾ) is the subject and "the Fire" its predicate.

﴿In it is the abode of eternity﴾: i.e., how is it said "in it"? The meaning is that it is the abode of eternity, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Certainly there was for you in the Messenger of God an excellent example﴾ [al-Ahzab: 21], and the Messenger himself is the example. The poet said:

"And in God, if they do not act justly, is a just judge"

The meaning is that God is the just Judge.

The figurative sense of this is that a thing may be made a container for itself, by considering its relation (mutaʿallaq), as an intensification, as if that relation became the thing's place of settlement. This is more emphatic than attributing that relation to it by way of informing about it.

﴿A recompense for what they used to deny Our signs﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: their recompense is for what they used to engage in idle talk about in it, so he mentioned denial, which is the cause of the idle talk. When the disbelievers saw the magnitude of the punishment of the Fire that had befallen them, they asked God, exalted is He, to show them the one who had been the cause of their misguidance and leading astray. The apparent meaning is that "those who" (alladhayn) is intended as a genus, i.e., every misleader of these two kinds. It is reported from ʿAli and Qatada that they are Iblis and Qabil: Iblis instituted disbelief, and Qabil instituted killing without right.

It was said: Is this statement from ʿAli sound? Qabil was a believing sinner, and they only sought those who misled them into disbelief, which leads to eternity. This statement has been reconciled by saying: Qabil sought every sinner among the people of major sins, and Iblis sought every disbeliever. The wording of the verse rejects this statement and its reconciliation. The disagreement over the reading of (arina) in His saying: ﴿And show us our rites﴾ [al-Baqarah: 128] has already been mentioned.

Al-Zamakhshari said: They related from al-Khalil that if you say arini thawbaka with a kasra, the meaning is "let me see it," and if you say it with sukun, it is a request for gifts, meaning "give me your garment." Its parallel is the common use of ityaʾ in the sense of iʿtaʾ, whose original meaning is "bringing." End.

﴿We will put them beneath our feet﴾: they mean at the lowest level of the Fire, which is more severe in punishment, and it is the abode of the hypocrites.

The doubling of the nun in alladhayni, allatayni, hadhayni and hatayni when they are in the oblique case with ya' is not permitted by the Basrians, and the reading with it in the seven readers is a proof against them.

(p-496) Ibn Abbas said: It was revealed concerning al-Siddiq (Abu Bakr). The polytheists said, "Our Lord is Allah, and the angels are His daughters, and these are our intercessors with Him." The Jews said, "Our Lord is Allah, and Ezra (al-'Uzayr) is His son, and Muhammad is not a prophet." So they did not remain upright. But al-Siddiq said, "Our Lord is Allah alone, without partner, and Muhammad is His servant and messenger," and so he remained upright.

When Allah, exalted is He, had elaborated on the threat against the disbelievers, He followed it with a promise for the believers. What is meant is not merely the utterance of words, but there must be belief that corresponds to the spoken word. He began first with that which is most fundamental in Islam, which is knowledge of the lordship (rububiyya) of Allah, and then followed it with righteous deeds, which is steadfastness (istiqama).

It is narrated from Sufyan ibn Abdullah al-Thaqafi that he said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Tell me a matter to which I may hold fast." He said: "Say, 'My Lord is Allah,' then be steadfast." I said: "What is the thing you fear most for me?" The Messenger of Allah ﷺ took hold of his own tongue and said: "This."

From al-Siddiq: "Then they remained steadfast" means they remained steadfast upon monotheism (tawhid), and their faith was not shaken. From Umar: they were steadfast for Allah by obeying Him, not evading [His commands] as foxes evade. From Uthman: they made their deeds sincere. From Ali: they performed the obligatory duties (fara'id).

Abu al-Aliya and al-Suddi said: they remained steadfast in sincerity and in action until death. al-Thawri said: they acted in accordance with what they had said. al-Fadl said: they renounced the transient world and desired the lasting one. al-Rabi' said: they turned away from everything other than Allah, exalted is He.

It was also said: they were steadfast in deed as they were steadfast in word. From al-Hasan, Qatada, and a group: they were steadfast in acts of obedience and in avoiding sins.

al-Zamakhshari said: "Thumma" (then) indicates that the steadfastness is distant in rank from the mere affirmation [of faith], and it is given precedence over it, because steadfastness has all the importance. A similar usage is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The believers are only those who have believed in Allah and His Messenger, then did not doubt﴾. The meaning is: then they held firm to the affirmation and what it requires. It is narrated from al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, that he recited it and then said: "What do you say about it?" They said: "They did not commit sins." He said: "You have taken the matter to its extreme." They said: "Then what do you say?" He said: "They did not return to the worship of idols." End of quote.

﴿The angels descend upon them﴾: Mujahid and al-Suddi said: at death. Muqatil said: at the resurrection. It was also said: at death, in the grave, and at the resurrection. Here "an" (أنْ) is a particle that governs the imperfect verb (nasiba li-l-mudari'), meaning: "by the absence of your fear and your grief." This was said by al-Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa'.

al-Zamakhshari said: it has the meaning of "ay" (أيْ, that is), or it is the light form (mukhaffafa) of the heavy "inna," and its original form is "bi-annahu la takhafu," with the pronoun "ha'" being the pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n). End of quote. According to these two interpretations, the verb is in the jussive mood after the prohibitive "la" (لا). This is a general verse for every future concern and a complete consolation for every past loss. Therefore Mujahid said: "Do not fear" what you have power over, and ﴿nor grieve﴾ over what you have left behind of your worldly life.

Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: "Do not fear" the rejection of your reward, for it is accepted; "nor grieve" over your sins, for I shall forgive them for you.

In the reading of Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud), it is "la takhafu" (without "an"), meaning: ﴿the angels descend upon them﴾ saying, "Do not fear and do not grieve."

Since fear of what is expected of harm is greater than grief over what has been lost, He mentioned it first. Then, when security was established for them, they were given good news of what they would attain, namely entry into Paradise. Thus they obtained complete security and great joy concerning the good they would do.

﴿We are your allies (awliya')﴾: The apparent meaning is that this is from the speech of the angels, meaning they say to them. In the reading of Abdullah, it forms part of what was said before, meaning: "We were your allies in the world, and we are your allies in the Hereafter."

Since the allies (awliya') of the disbelievers are their companions from the devils, the allies of the believers are the angels.

al-Suddi said: "We are your guardians (hafaza) in the world, and your allies in the Hereafter." It was also said: ﴿We are your allies﴾ is from the speech of Allah, exalted is He, meaning allies in sufficiency and guidance. ﴿And for you therein﴾: the pronoun refers to the Hereafter, as Ibn Atiyya said. al-Hawfi said it refers to Paradise.

﴿What your souls desire﴾ of pleasures, ﴿and for you therein is what you call for﴾. Muqatil said: what you wish for. It was also said: what you want. Ibn Isa said: whatever you claim is yours, it is yours by the decree of your Lord. Ibn Atiyya said: what you request.

﴿As a hospitable gift (nuzulan) from a Forgiving, Merciful [One]﴾: "Nuzul" is the provision prepared for a guest (nazil), who is the visitor. Ibn Ata' said this, so "nuzulan" is then a circumstantial accusative (hal), meaning you are given that in the state of being a provision, not as a [mere] gift. Some have made it a verbal noun from "anzala."

It was also said that "nuzul" is the plural of "nazil," like "sharif" and "shurf," so it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state, meaning "descending/arriving," and the subject of the state is the pronoun in "yad'una." al-Hasan said: the meaning of "nuzulan" is "from Us." It was also said: a reward. Abu Haywa read it as "nuzlan" with the zay sukun.

Since His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, those who have said, "Our Lord is Allah," then remained steadfast﴾ has preceded, He mentioned the one who calls to that, saying: ﴿And who is better in speech than one who invites to Allah and does righteous deeds and says, "Indeed I am of the Muslims"?﴾ That is, no one is better in speech than the one who calls to the monotheism of Allah, does righteous deeds, and declares that he is among those who submit to the command of Allah and comply with Him. The apparent meaning is general for every caller to Allah, and al-Hasan, Muqatil, and a group held this general view. It was also said that it is specific: Ibn Abbas said it is the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who called to Islam, did righteous deeds between himself and his Lord, and made Islam a faith. He also said from him: they are the companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

Aisha, Qays ibn Abi Hazim, Ikrima, and Mujahid said: it was revealed concerning the muezzins (mu'adhdhinun). Their statement should be interpreted as meaning that they are included in the verse; otherwise, the surah in its entirety is Meccan without any disagreement. The call to prayer (adhan) was not in Mecca; it was legislated in Medina. The call to Allah is by calling to Islam, by fighting the disbelievers, and by restraining the oppressors.

Zayd ibn Ali said: he called to Allah by the sword, and this—Allah knows best—is what prompted him to rise with the sword against some of the oppressive rulers of the Banu Umayya.

This Zayd was a scholar of the Book of Allah, and I have come across a portion of his exegesis of the Book of Allah, and his delivering it to some of those who transmitted from him while he was imprisoned by Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik. It contains a great share of knowledge and citation of the speech of the Arabs. It is said that when he and his brother Muhammad al-Baqir debated, people gathered with inkwells, writing down what proceeded from them of knowledge. May Allah have mercy on them both and be pleased with them.

Abu al-Aliya said: ﴿and does righteous deeds﴾: he prayed between the adhan and the iqama. Ikrima said: he prayed and fasted. al-Kalbi said: he performed the obligatory duties. Mujahid said: it is general for everyone who combines these three: being a monotheist, holding the faith of Islam, acting in goodness, and calling to it. Their final destination is the rank of the knowledgeable who act, from among the people of justice (adl) and monotheism (tawhid), the callers to the religion of Islam. End of quote. He means by this the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school), who call themselves "the people of justice and monotheism," and this is found in their poetry, as Ibn Abi al-Hadid the Mu'tazili, author of the book "al-Falak al-Da'ir fi al-Radd 'ala Kitab al-Mathal al-Sa'ir," said in his words. He said: The Imam, the memorizer (al-hafiz) Sharaf al-Din Abd al-Mu'min ibn Khalaf al-Dimyati, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him, recited to us from him:

Were it not for three, I would not fear my downfall, which is not as the youth of the slave said:
That I support monotheism and justice in every station, exerting my utmost effort;
And that I converse with Allah, enjoying a solitude sweeter than honey;
And that I rise up proudly against every base person with a sneering face.
For that I desire, not a young woman nor wine nor one with a shapely, full-bosomed figure.

﴿And said, "Indeed I am of the Muslims"﴾: The meaning is not that he uttered these words, but that he made Islam his creed. Just as you say, "This is the saying of al-Shafi'i," meaning his doctrine.

Ibn Abi Ablah and Ibrahim ibn Nuh, from Qutayba al-Mayyal, read "wa qala inni" with a single doubled nun; the majority read "inanni" with it and with the nun of protection (nun al-wiqaya).

Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi said: no condition was stipulated except "if Allah wills," so this is a refutation of those who say, "I am a Muslim, if Allah wills."

When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned that no one is better than the one who calls to Allah, He mentioned what follows from that of good character, and that the caller to Allah may be met with harshness by the one he calls, so he should be gentle with him and kind in conveying the good to him (p-498).

It was said: it was revealed concerning Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, who had been an enemy of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and then became a sincere ally.

Ibn Abbas said: "the good deed" is "there is no god but Allah," and "the evil deed" is polytheism (shirk). al-Kalbi said: the two calls to them.

al-Dahhak said: forbearance and foul speech. From Ali: love of the Messenger and his household and hatred of their enemies. It was said: patience and aversion.

It was said: tolerance and harshness. It was said: pardon and moderation. These are examples of the good and the evil, not a restrictive enumeration.

Since the good and the evil differ, He commanded that the evil be repelled with what is better, and this is for emphasis. He did not say, "Repel the evil with the good," because whoever finds it easy to repel with the better will find it easy to repel with the good. That is, when you do that, ﴿then he between whom and you is enmity﴾ becomes for you like a close friend, a loyal ally of sincere friendship. The "la" (لا) in His saying ﴿nor is the evil﴾ is an extra particle for emphasis, just as it is in His saying ﴿nor is the shade [equal to] the heat﴾ [Fatir 35:21], because "istawa" (to be equal) does not suffice with a single noun. The one of the good and the evil is a category, so its addition would not be like its addition in the previous aspect, for the meaning would become: "the good deeds are not equal," since they vary in themselves, "nor the evil deeds," because they too vary.

Ibn Atiyya said: "ka'anna" (as if) came for comparison, because the one who has enmity does not become a warm, loyal ally, but his outward appearance becomes good, so he is likened to the warm ally.

From Ibn Abbas: ﴿with that which is better﴾ means patience when angry, forbearance when ignorant, and pardon when wronged.

Mujahid and Ata' said: greeting at the time of meeting. End of quote. That is, it is the starting point of repelling with what is better, because it is confined to it.

Also from Mujahid: turn away from their harm. Abu Firas al-Hamdani said:

He wrongs me, and I bend, always greeting him with a face of welcome.
Nothing is better than one side turned toward the other side.

And none is granted it except those who are patient, and none is granted it except one of great fortune.

[Translation of the passage follows.]

**﴿وما يُلَقّاها﴾**: The pronoun refers to the act and the disposition, which is repelling evil with what is better. Talha ibn Musarrif and Ibn Kathir, in one transmission, read ﴿وما يُلَقّاها﴾ from al-mulaqah (encountering). The majority read it from al-taladdi (receiving). It is as if this noble trait is absent, so none encounters it or is granted it by God except one who is patient in acts of obedience, restraining himself from desires, and possessing a great share of the qualities of goodness. This is said by Ibn Abbas, and it is then praise. Or (ذُو حَظٍّ عَظِيمٍ) means a great share of the reward of the Hereafter, said by Qatada, and then it is a promise. It is also said: except one of intellect. And it is said: one of good character. He repeated ﴿وما يُلَقّاها﴾ to emphasise this beautiful and sublime act. It is also said that the pronoun in (يُلَقّاها) refers to Paradise.

Makki related: ﴿وما يُلَقّاها﴾ means the testimony that there is no god but God, but this is far-fetched.

When God commanded repelling evil with what is better, a Muslim may at times be inclined to respond to one who has wronged him with evil. So He commanded him, if this arises in him, to seek refuge in God, for that is a prick of Satan (نَزْغ الشَّيْطانِ, a prompting of Satan). The explanation of the like of this verse has already been given at the end of al-A'raf.

When God made clear that the best of deeds and words is the like of this verse, which is calling to God, He followed it with mention of the signs above and below, of His overpowering power, His perfect wisdom, and His decisive proof. He began with mention of the celestial matters, night and day, and He placed the mention of night first. It is said: as a reminder that darkness is an absence and light is an existence. The mention of the sun after the day is fitting, because it is the cause of its illumination and by it the world appears, and because it is more effective in illumination than the moon, and because the moon, as they say, derives its light from the light of the sun.

Then God forbade prostration to them both, and commanded prostration to the Creator, exalted is He.

Some people used to worship the sun, as is mentioned in the story of Bilqis and her people. The pronoun in (خَلَقَهُنَّ) refers to the night, the day, the sun and the moon.

Al-Zamakhshari said: because the rule for a plural of non-rational things is the rule of the feminine, i.e., feminine forms, one says: "al-aqlam, I sharpened them" and "bariytuhunna" (I sharpened them, feminine). He ended, meaning non-rational masculine nouns. He should have distinguished among the plural of paucity in this, for the more eloquent usage is that it is treated like the pronoun of the feminine singular: one says "al-ajdha'u inkasarat" (the trunks broke) in the most eloquent usage, and "al-judhu'u inkasarna" (the trunks broke, feminine plural) in the most eloquent usage.

What precedes in the verse is not a plural of paucity in a single form; rather, it mentions four items joined by conjunction, so they are placed in the position of a plural expressed by a single word.

Al-Zamakhshari also said: when He said ﴿ومِن آياتِهِ﴾ (and among His signs), they were in the sense of signs, so it was said ﴿خَلَقَهُنَّ﴾ (He created them, feminine plural). He ended, meaning: the sense is "the night, the day, the sun and the moon are among His signs," so the pronoun returns to the plural "signs" implied in the genitive. It is also said that it returns to the signs mentioned previously. It is also said that it returns to the sun and the moon, and the dual is a plural, and the plural of non-rational things takes the feminine; and since it is said "shumus" and "aqmar" (suns and moons), because they differ by days and nights, it is permissible for the pronoun to return in the plural.

﴿إنْ كُنْتُمْ إيّاهُ تَعْبُدُونَ﴾ means: if you are monotheists, not associators.

The prostration, according to al-Shafi'i, is at (تَعْبُدُونَ) (you worship), and this is the transmission of Masruq from Abdullah, because the word "prostration" is mentioned before it. According to Abu Hanifa it is at ﴿لا يَسْأمُونَ﴾ (they do not tire), because it completes the meaning. In al-Tahrir: Ali and Ibn Mas'ud used to prostrate at (تَعْبُدُونَ). Ibn Wahb and al-Shafi'i said: at ﴿يَسْأمُونَ﴾, and Abu Hanifa also held this view. Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar, Abu Wa'il, Bakr ibn Abdullah prostrated there, and likewise it is related from Masruq, al-Sulami, al-Nakha'i, Abu Salih and Ibn Sirin. He ended, summarized.

﴿فَإنِ اسْتَكْبَرُوا﴾ means: they magnified themselves, refusing to avoid what I forbade of prostrating to these two created, ordered beings, and to comply with what I commanded of prostrating to the Creator of them; for the angels, who are with God in noble rank and station, glorify Him above what does not befit His majesty, ﴿وهم لا يَسْأمُونَ﴾ means they do not weary of that. And they are better than you, while God is free of need of your worship and of theirs.

When He mentioned some of the celestial signs, He mentioned some of the terrestrial signs, saying: ﴿ومِن آياتِهِ أنَّكَ تَرى الأرْضَ خاشِعَةً﴾ meaning: dusty and effaced, as the poet said:

*And a stone-ring like the trunk of a pool, faded and humble.*

Humility (al-khushu') is borrowed for it, which is submission because of the drought, absence of vegetation and hardship of life that appear in it, unlike when it is verdant with plants, flowering and fruitful trees, for that is its life.

Al-Sudi said: (خاشِعَةً) means dead and dry. The discussion of ﴿فَإذا أنْزَلْنا عَلَيْها الماءَ اهْتَزَّتْ ورَبَتْ﴾ (then when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells) has already been given, both in interpretation and recitation, at the beginning of Surat al-Hajj.

﴿إنَّ الَّذِي أحْياها لَمُحْيِي المَوْتى﴾: He who gives it life is surely the giver of life to the dead, returning souls to bodies. ﴿إنَّهُ عَلى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ﴾: nothing overcomes Him, on anything whatever upon which His will is set.

(p-496) Ibn Abbas said: It was revealed concerning al-Siddiq (Abu Bakr). The polytheists said, "Our Lord is Allah, and the angels are His daughters, and these are our intercessors with Him." The Jews said, "Our Lord is Allah, and Ezra (al-'Uzayr) is His son, and Muhammad is not a prophet." So they did not remain upright. But al-Siddiq said, "Our Lord is Allah alone, without partner, and Muhammad is His servant and messenger," and so he remained upright.

When Allah, exalted is He, had elaborated on the threat against the disbelievers, He followed it with a promise for the believers. What is meant is not merely the utterance of words, but there must be belief that corresponds to the spoken word. He began first with that which is most fundamental in Islam, which is knowledge of the lordship (rububiyya) of Allah, and then followed it with righteous deeds, which is steadfastness (istiqama).

It is narrated from Sufyan ibn Abdullah al-Thaqafi that he said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Tell me a matter to which I may hold fast." He said: "Say, 'My Lord is Allah,' then be steadfast." I said: "What is the thing you fear most for me?" The Messenger of Allah ﷺ took hold of his own tongue and said: "This."

From al-Siddiq: "Then they remained steadfast" means they remained steadfast upon monotheism (tawhid), and their faith was not shaken. From Umar: they were steadfast for Allah by obeying Him, not evading [His commands] as foxes evade. From Uthman: they made their deeds sincere. From Ali: they performed the obligatory duties (fara'id).

Abu al-Aliya and al-Suddi said: they remained steadfast in sincerity and in action until death. al-Thawri said: they acted in accordance with what they had said. al-Fadl said: they renounced the transient world and desired the lasting one. al-Rabi' said: they turned away from everything other than Allah, exalted is He.

It was also said: they were steadfast in deed as they were steadfast in word. From al-Hasan, Qatada, and a group: they were steadfast in acts of obedience and in avoiding sins.

al-Zamakhshari said: "Thumma" (then) indicates that the steadfastness is distant in rank from the mere affirmation [of faith], and it is given precedence over it, because steadfastness has all the importance. A similar usage is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The believers are only those who have believed in Allah and His Messenger, then did not doubt﴾. The meaning is: then they held firm to the affirmation and what it requires. It is narrated from al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, that he recited it and then said: "What do you say about it?" They said: "They did not commit sins." He said: "You have taken the matter to its extreme." They said: "Then what do you say?" He said: "They did not return to the worship of idols." End of quote.

﴿The angels descend upon them﴾: Mujahid and al-Suddi said: at death. Muqatil said: at the resurrection. It was also said: at death, in the grave, and at the resurrection. Here "an" (أنْ) is a particle that governs the imperfect verb (nasiba li-l-mudari'), meaning: "by the absence of your fear and your grief." This was said by al-Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa'.

al-Zamakhshari said: it has the meaning of "ay" (أيْ, that is), or it is the light form (mukhaffafa) of the heavy "inna," and its original form is "bi-annahu la takhafu," with the pronoun "ha'" being the pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n). End of quote. According to these two interpretations, the verb is in the jussive mood after the prohibitive "la" (لا). This is a general verse for every future concern and a complete consolation for every past loss. Therefore Mujahid said: "Do not fear" what you have power over, and ﴿nor grieve﴾ over what you have left behind of your worldly life.

Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: "Do not fear" the rejection of your reward, for it is accepted; "nor grieve" over your sins, for I shall forgive them for you.

In the reading of Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud), it is "la takhafu" (without "an"), meaning: ﴿the angels descend upon them﴾ saying, "Do not fear and do not grieve."

Since fear of what is expected of harm is greater than grief over what has been lost, He mentioned it first. Then, when security was established for them, they were given good news of what they would attain, namely entry into Paradise. Thus they obtained complete security and great joy concerning the good they would do.

﴿We are your allies (awliya')﴾: The apparent meaning is that this is from the speech of the angels, meaning they say to them. In the reading of Abdullah, it forms part of what was said before, meaning: "We were your allies in the world, and we are your allies in the Hereafter."

Since the allies (awliya') of the disbelievers are their companions from the devils, the allies of the believers are the angels.

al-Suddi said: "We are your guardians (hafaza) in the world, and your allies in the Hereafter." It was also said: ﴿We are your allies﴾ is from the speech of Allah, exalted is He, meaning allies in sufficiency and guidance. ﴿And for you therein﴾: the pronoun refers to the Hereafter, as Ibn Atiyya said. al-Hawfi said it refers to Paradise.

﴿What your souls desire﴾ of pleasures, ﴿and for you therein is what you call for﴾. Muqatil said: what you wish for. It was also said: what you want. Ibn Isa said: whatever you claim is yours, it is yours by the decree of your Lord. Ibn Atiyya said: what you request.

﴿As a hospitable gift (nuzulan) from a Forgiving, Merciful [One]﴾: "Nuzul" is the provision prepared for a guest (nazil), who is the visitor. Ibn Ata' said this, so "nuzulan" is then a circumstantial accusative (hal), meaning you are given that in the state of being a provision, not as a [mere] gift. Some have made it a verbal noun from "anzala."

It was also said that "nuzul" is the plural of "nazil," like "sharif" and "shurf," so it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state, meaning "descending/arriving," and the subject of the state is the pronoun in "yad'una." al-Hasan said: the meaning of "nuzulan" is "from Us." It was also said: a reward. Abu Haywa read it as "nuzlan" with the zay sukun.

Since His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, those who have said, "Our Lord is Allah," then remained steadfast﴾ has preceded, He mentioned the one who calls to that, saying: ﴿And who is better in speech than one who invites to Allah and does righteous deeds and says, "Indeed I am of the Muslims"?﴾ That is, no one is better in speech than the one who calls to the monotheism of Allah, does righteous deeds, and declares that he is among those who submit to the command of Allah and comply with Him. The apparent meaning is general for every caller to Allah, and al-Hasan, Muqatil, and a group held this general view. It was also said that it is specific: Ibn Abbas said it is the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who called to Islam, did righteous deeds between himself and his Lord, and made Islam a faith. He also said from him: they are the companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

Aisha, Qays ibn Abi Hazim, Ikrima, and Mujahid said: it was revealed concerning the muezzins (mu'adhdhinun). Their statement should be interpreted as meaning that they are included in the verse; otherwise, the surah in its entirety is Meccan without any disagreement. The call to prayer (adhan) was not in Mecca; it was legislated in Medina. The call to Allah is by calling to Islam, by fighting the disbelievers, and by restraining the oppressors.

Zayd ibn Ali said: he called to Allah by the sword, and this—Allah knows best—is what prompted him to rise with the sword against some of the oppressive rulers of the Banu Umayya.

This Zayd was a scholar of the Book of Allah, and I have come across a portion of his exegesis of the Book of Allah, and his delivering it to some of those who transmitted from him while he was imprisoned by Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik. It contains a great share of knowledge and citation of the speech of the Arabs. It is said that when he and his brother Muhammad al-Baqir debated, people gathered with inkwells, writing down what proceeded from them of knowledge. May Allah have mercy on them both and be pleased with them.

Abu al-Aliya said: ﴿and does righteous deeds﴾: he prayed between the adhan and the iqama. Ikrima said: he prayed and fasted. al-Kalbi said: he performed the obligatory duties. That I support monotheism and justice in every station, exerting my utmost effort;

According to Abu Hanifa it is at ﴿لا يَسْأمُونَ﴾ (they do not tire), because it completes the meaning. In al-Tahrir: Ali and Ibn Mas'ud used to prostrate at (تَعْبُدُونَ). Ibn Wahb and al-Shafi'i said: at ﴿يَسْأمُونَ﴾, and Abu Hanifa also held this view. Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar, Abu Wa'il, Bakr ibn Abdullah prostrated there, and likewise it is related from Masruq, al-Sulami, al-Nakha'i, Abu Salih and Ibn Sirin. He ended, summarized.

﴿فَإنِ اسْتَكْبَرُوا﴾ means: they magnified themselves, refusing to avoid what I forbade of prostrating to these two created, ordered beings, and to comply with what I commanded of prostrating to the Creator of them; for the angels, who are with God in noble rank and station, glorify Him above what does not befit His majesty, ﴿وهم لا يَسْأمُونَ﴾ means they do not weary of that. And they are better than you, while God is free of need of your worship and of theirs.

When He mentioned some of the celestial signs, He mentioned some of the terrestrial signs, saying: ﴿ومِن آياتِهِ أنَّكَ تَرى الأرْضَ خاشِعَةً﴾ meaning: dusty and effaced, as the poet said:

*And a stone-ring like the trunk of a pool, faded and humble.*

Humility (al-khushu') is borrowed for it, which is submission because of the drought, absence of vegetation and hardship of life that appear in it, unlike when it is verdant with plants, flowering and fruitful trees, for that is its life.

Al-Sudi said: (خاشِعَةً) means dead and dry. The discussion of ﴿فَإذا أنْزَلْنا عَلَيْها الماءَ اهْتَزَّتْ ورَبَتْ﴾ (then when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells) has already been given, both in interpretation and recitation, at the beginning of Surat al-Hajj.

﴿إنَّ الَّذِي أحْياها لَمُحْيِي المَوْتى﴾: He who gives it life is surely the giver of life to the dead, returning souls to bodies. ﴿إنَّهُ عَلى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ﴾: nothing overcomes Him, on anything whatever upon which His will is set.

(p-496) Ibn Abbas said: It was revealed concerning al-Siddiq (Abu Bakr). The polytheists said, "Our Lord is Allah, and the angels are His daughters, and these are our intercessors with Him." The Jews said, "Our Lord is Allah, and Ezra (al-'Uzayr) is His son, and Muhammad is not a prophet." So they did not remain upright. But al-Siddiq said, "Our Lord is Allah alone, without partner, and Muhammad is His servant and messenger," and so he remained upright.

When Allah, exalted is He, had elaborated on the threat against the disbelievers, He followed it with a promise for the believers. What is meant is not merely the utterance of words, but there must be belief that corresponds to the spoken word. He began first with that which is most fundamental in Islam, which is knowledge of the lordship (rububiyya) of Allah, and then followed it with righteous deeds, which is steadfastness (istiqama).

It is narrated from Sufyan ibn Abdullah al-Thaqafi that he said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Tell me a matter to which I may hold fast." He said: "Say, 'My Lord is Allah,' then be steadfast." I said: "What is the thing you fear most for me?" The Messenger of Allah ﷺ took hold of his own tongue and said: "This."

From al-Siddiq: "Then they remained steadfast" means they remained steadfast upon monotheism (tawhid), and their faith was not shaken. From Umar: they were steadfast for Allah by obeying Him, not evading [His commands] as foxes evade. From Uthman: they made their deeds sincere. From Ali: they performed the obligatory duties (fara'id).

Abu al-Aliya and al-Suddi said: they remained steadfast in sincerity and in action until death. al-Thawri said: they acted in accordance with what they had said. al-Fadl said: they renounced the transient world and desired the lasting one. al-Rabi' said: they turned away from everything other than Allah, exalted is He.

It was also said: they were steadfast in deed as they were steadfast in word. From al-Hasan, Qatada, and a group: they were steadfast in acts of obedience and in avoiding sins.

al-Zamakhshari said: "Thumma" (then) indicates that the steadfastness is distant in rank from the mere affirmation [of faith], and it is given precedence over it, because steadfastness has all the importance. A similar usage is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The believers are only those who have believed in Allah and His Messenger, then did not doubt﴾. The meaning is: then they held firm to the affirmation and what it requires. It is narrated from al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, that he recited it and then said: "What do you say about it?" They said: "They did not commit sins." He said: "You have taken the matter to its extreme." They said: "Then what do you say?" He said: "They did not return to the worship of idols." End of quote.

﴿The angels descend upon them﴾: Mujahid and al-Suddi said: at death. Muqatil said: at the resurrection. It was also said: at death, in the grave, and at the resurrection. Here "an" (أنْ) is a particle that governs the imperfect verb (nasiba li-l-mudari'), meaning: "by the absence of your fear and your grief." This was said by al-Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa'.

al-Zamakhshari said: it has the meaning of "ay" (أيْ, that is), or it is the light form (mukhaffafa) of the heavy "inna," and its original form is "bi-annahu la takhafu," with the pronoun "ha'" being the pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n). End of quote. According to these two interpretations, the verb is in the jussive mood after the prohibitive "la" (لا). This is a general verse for every future concern and a complete consolation for every past loss. Therefore Mujahid said: "Do not fear" what you have power over, and ﴿nor grieve﴾ over what you have left behind of your worldly life.

Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: "Do not fear" the rejection of your reward, for it is accepted; "nor grieve" over your sins, for I shall forgive them for you.

In the reading of Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud), it is "la takhafu" (without "an"), meaning: ﴿the angels descend upon them﴾ saying, "Do not fear and do not grieve."

Since fear of what is expected of harm is greater than grief over what has been lost, He mentioned it first. Then, when security was established for them, they were given good news of what they would attain, namely entry into Paradise. Thus they obtained complete security and great joy concerning the good they would do.

﴿We are your allies (awliya')﴾: The apparent meaning is that this is from the speech of the angels, meaning they say to them. In the reading of Abdullah, it forms part of what was said before, meaning: "We were your allies in the world, and we are your allies in the Hereafter."

Since the allies (awliya') of the disbelievers are their companions from the devils, the allies of the believers are the angels.

al-Suddi said: "We are your guardians (hafaza) in the world, and your allies in the Hereafter." It was also said: ﴿We are your allies﴾ is from the speech of Allah, exalted is He, meaning allies in sufficiency and guidance. ﴿And for you therein﴾: the pronoun refers to the Hereafter, as Ibn Atiyya said. al-Hawfi said it refers to Paradise.

﴿What your souls desire﴾ of pleasures, ﴿and for you therein is what you call for﴾. Muqatil said: what you wish for. It was also said: what you want. Ibn Isa said: whatever you claim is yours, it is yours by the decree of your Lord. Ibn Atiyya said: what you request.

﴿As a hospitable gift (nuzulan) from a Forgiving, Merciful [One]﴾: "Nuzul" is the provision prepared for a guest (nazil), who is the visitor. Ibn Ata' said this, so "nuzulan" is then a circumstantial accusative (hal), meaning you are given that in the state of being a provision, not as a [mere] gift. Some have made it a verbal noun from "anzala."

It was also said that "nuzul" is the plural of "nazil," like "sharif" and "shurf," so it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state, meaning "descending/arriving," and the subject of the state is the pronoun in "yad'una." al-Hasan said: the meaning of "nuzulan" is "from Us." It was also said: a reward. Abu Haywa read it as "nuzlan" with the zay sukun.

Since His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, those who have said, "Our Lord is Allah," then remained steadfast﴾ has preceded, He mentioned the one who calls to that, saying: ﴿And who is better in speech than one who invites to Allah and does righteous deeds and says, "Indeed I am of the Muslims"?﴾ That is, no one is better in speech than the one who calls to the monotheism of Allah, does righteous deeds, and declares that he is among those who submit to the command of Allah and comply with Him. The apparent meaning is general for every caller to Allah, and al-Hasan, Muqatil, and a group held this general view. It was also said that it is specific: Ibn Abbas said it is the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who called to Islam, did righteous deeds between himself and his Lord, and made Islam a faith. He also said from him: they are the companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

Aisha, Qays ibn Abi Hazim, Ikrima, and Mujahid said: it was revealed concerning the muezzins (mu'adhdhinun). Their statement should be interpreted as meaning that they are included in the verse; otherwise, the surah in its entirety is Meccan without any disagreement. The call to prayer (adhan) was not in Mecca; it was legislated in Medina. The call to Allah is by calling to Islam, by fighting the disbelievers, and by restraining the oppressors.

Zayd ibn Ali said: he called to Allah by the sword, and this—Allah knows best—is what prompted him to rise with the sword against some of the oppressive rulers of the Banu Umayya.

This Zayd was a scholar of the Book of Allah, and I have come across a portion of his exegesis of the Book of Allah, and his delivering it to some of those who transmitted from him while he was imprisoned by Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik. It contains a great share of knowledge and citation of the speech of the Arabs. It is said that when he and his brother Muhammad al-Baqir debated, people gathered with inkwells, writing down what proceeded from them of knowledge. May Allah have mercy on them both and be pleased with them.

Abu al-Aliya said: ﴿and does righteous deeds﴾: he prayed between the adhan and the iqama. Ikrima said: he prayed and fasted. al-Kalbi said: he performed the obligatory duties. Mujahid said: it is general for everyone who combines these three: being a monotheist, holding the faith of Islam, acting in goodness, and calling to it. Their final destination is the rank of the knowledgeable who act, from among the people of justice (adl) and monotheism (tawhid), the callers to the religion of Islam. End of quote. He means by this the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school), who call themselves "the people of justice and monotheism," and this is found in their poetry, as Ibn Abi al-Hadid the Mu'tazili, author of the book "al-Falak al-Da'ir fi al-Radd 'ala Kitab al-Mathal al-Sa'ir," said in his words. He said: The Imam, the memorizer (al-hafiz) Sharaf al-Din Abd al-Mu'min ibn Khalaf al-Dimyati, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him, recited to us from him:

Were it not for three, I would not fear my downfall, which is not as the youth of the slave said:
That I support monotheism and justice in every station, exerting my utmost effort;
And that I converse with Allah, enjoying a solitude sweeter than honey;
And that I rise up proudly against every base person with a sneering face.
For that I desire, not a young woman nor wine nor one with a shapely, full-bosomed figure.

﴿And said, "Indeed I am of the Muslims"﴾: The meaning is not that he uttered these words, but that he made Islam his creed. Just as you say, "This is the saying of al-Shafi'i," meaning his doctrine.

Ibn Abi Ablah and Ibrahim ibn Nuh, from Qutayba al-Mayyal, read "wa qala inni" with a single doubled nun; the majority read "inanni" with it and with the nun of protection (nun al-wiqaya).

Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi said: no condition was stipulated except "if Allah wills," so this is a refutation of those who say, "I am a Muslim, if Allah wills."

When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned that no one is better than the one who calls to Allah, He mentioned what follows from that of good character, and that the caller to Allah may be met with harshness by the one he calls, so he should be gentle with him and kind in conveying the good to him (p-498).

It was said: it was revealed concerning Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, who had been an enemy of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and then became a sincere ally.

Ibn Abbas said: "the good deed" is "there is no god but Allah," and "the evil deed" is polytheism (shirk). al-Kalbi said: the two calls to them.

al-Dahhak said: forbearance and foul speech. From Ali: love of the Messenger and his household and hatred of their enemies. It was said: patience and aversion.

It was said: tolerance and harshness. It was said: pardon and moderation. These are examples of the good and the evil, not a restrictive enumeration.

Since the good and the evil differ, He commanded that the evil be repelled with what is better, and this is for emphasis. He did not say, "Repel the evil with the good," because whoever finds it easy to repel with the better will find it easy to repel with the good. That is, when you do that, ﴿then he between whom and you is enmity﴾ becomes for you like a close friend, a loyal ally of sincere friendship. The "la" (لا) in His saying ﴿nor is the evil﴾ is an extra particle for emphasis, just as it is in His saying ﴿nor is the shade [equal to] the heat﴾ [Fatir 35:21], because "istawa" (to be equal) does not suffice with a single noun. The one of the good and the evil is a category, so its addition would not be like its addition in the previous aspect, for the meaning would become: "the good deeds are not equal," since they vary in themselves, "nor the evil deeds," because they too vary.

Ibn Atiyya said: "ka'anna" (as if) came for comparison, because the one who has enmity does not become a warm, loyal ally, but his outward appearance becomes good, so he is likened to the warm ally.

From Ibn Abbas: ﴿with that which is better﴾ means patience when angry, forbearance when ignorant, and pardon when wronged.

Mujahid and Ata' said: greeting at the time of meeting. End of quote. That is, it is the starting point of repelling with what is better, because it is confined to it.

Also from Mujahid: turn away from their harm. Abu Firas al-Hamdani said:

He wrongs me, and I bend, always greeting him with a face of welcome.
Nothing is better than one side turned toward the other side.

And none is granted it except those who are patient, and none is granted it except one of great fortune.

[Translation of the passage follows.]

**﴿وما يُلَقّاها﴾**: The pronoun refers to the act and the disposition, which is repelling evil with what is better. Talha ibn Musarrif and Ibn Kathir, in one transmission, read ﴿وما يُلَقّاها﴾ from al-mulaqah (encountering). The majority read it from al-taladdi (receiving). It is as if this noble trait is absent, so none encounters it or is granted it by God except one who is patient in acts of obedience, restraining himself from desires, and possessing a great share of the qualities of goodness. This is said by Ibn Abbas, and it is then praise. Or (ذُو حَظٍّ عَظِيمٍ) means a great share of the reward of the Hereafter, said by Qatada, and then it is a promise. It is also said: except one of intellect. And it is said: one of good character. He repeated ﴿وما يُلَقّاها﴾ to emphasise this beautiful and sublime act. It is also said that the pronoun in (يُلَقّاها) refers to Paradise.

Makki related: ﴿وما يُلَقّاها﴾ means the testimony that there is no god but God, but this is far-fetched.

When God commanded repelling evil with what is better, a Muslim may at times be inclined to respond to one who has wronged him with evil. So He commanded him, if this arises in him, to seek refuge in God, for that is a prick of Satan (نَزْغ الشَّيْطانِ, a prompting of Satan). The explanation of the like of this verse has already been given at the end of al-A'raf.

When God made clear that the best of deeds and words is the like of this verse, which is calling to God, He followed it with mention of the signs above and below, of His overpowering power, His perfect wisdom, and His decisive proof. He began with mention of the celestial matters, night and day, and He placed the mention of night first. It is said: as a reminder that darkness is an absence and light is an existence. The mention of the sun after the day is fitting, because it is the cause of its illumination and by it the world appears, and because it is more effective in illumination than the moon, and because the moon, as they say, derives its light from the light of the sun.

Then God forbade prostration to them both, and commanded prostration to the Creator, exalted is He.

Some people used to worship the sun, as is mentioned in the story of Bilqis and her people. The pronoun in (خَلَقَهُنَّ) refers to the night, the day, the sun and the moon.

Al-Zamakhshari said: because the rule for a plural of non-rational things is the rule of the feminine, i.e., feminine forms, one says: "al-aqlam, I sharpened them" and "bariytuhunna" (I sharpened them, feminine). He ended, meaning non-rational masculine nouns. He should have distinguished among the plural of paucity in this, for the more eloquent usage is that it is treated like the pronoun of the feminine singular: one says "al-ajdha'u inkasarat" (the trunks broke) in the most eloquent usage, and "al-judhu'u inkasarna" (the trunks broke, feminine plural) in the most eloquent usage.

What precedes in the verse is not a plural of paucity in a single form; rather, it mentions four items joined by conjunction, so they are placed in the position of a plural expressed by a single word.

Al-Zamakhshari also said: when He said ﴿ومِن آياتِهِ﴾ (and among His signs), they were in the sense of signs, so it was said ﴿خَلَقَهُنَّ﴾ (He created them, feminine plural). He ended, meaning: the sense is "the night, the day, the sun and the moon are among His signs," so the pronoun returns to the plural "signs" implied in the genitive. It is also said that it returns to the signs mentioned previously. It is also said that it returns to the sun and the moon, and the dual is a plural, and the plural of non-rational things takes the feminine; and since it is said "shumus" and "aqmar" (suns and moons), because they differ by days and nights, it is permissible for the pronoun to return in the plural.

Since His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, those who have said, "Our Lord is Allah," then remained steadfast﴾ has preceded, He mentioned the one who calls to that, saying: ﴿And who is better in speech than one who invites to Allah and does righteous deeds and says, "Indeed I am of the Muslims"?﴾ That is, no one is better in speech than the one who calls to the monotheism of Allah, does righteous deeds, and declares that he is among those who submit to the command of Allah and comply with Him. The apparent meaning is general for every caller to Allah, and al-Hasan, Muqatil, and a group held this general view. It was also said that it is specific: Ibn Abbas said it is the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who called to Islam, did righteous deeds between himself and his Lord, and made Islam a faith. He also said from him: they are the companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

Aisha, Qays ibn Abi Hazim, Ikrima, and Mujahid said: it was revealed concerning the muezzins (mu'adhdhinun). Their statement should be interpreted as meaning that they are included in the verse; otherwise, the surah in its entirety is Meccan without any disagreement. The call to prayer (adhan) was not in Mecca; it was legislated in Medina. The call to Allah is by calling to Islam, by fighting the disbelievers, and by restraining the oppressors.

Zayd ibn Ali said: he called to Allah by the sword, and this—Allah knows best—is what prompted him to rise with the sword against some of the oppressive rulers of the Banu Umayya.

This Zayd was a scholar of the Book of Allah, and I have come across a portion of his exegesis of the Book of Allah, and his delivering it to some of those who transmitted from him while he was imprisoned by Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik. It contains a great share of knowledge and citation of the speech of the Arabs. It is said that when he and his brother Muhammad al-Baqir debated, people gathered with inkwells, writing down what proceeded from them of knowledge. May Allah have mercy on them both and be pleased with them.

Abu al-Aliya said: ﴿and does righteous deeds﴾: he prayed between the adhan and the iqama. Ikrima said: he prayed and fasted. al-Kalbi said: he performed the obligatory duties. Mujahid said: it is general for everyone who combines these three: being a monotheist, holding the faith of Islam, acting in goodness, and calling to it. Their final destination is the rank of the knowledgeable who act, from among the people of justice (adl) and monotheism (tawhid), the callers to the religion of Islam. End of quote. He means by this the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school), who call themselves "the people of justice and monotheism," and this is found in their poetry, as Ibn Abi al-Hadid the Mu'tazili, author of the book "al-Falak al-Da'ir fi al-Radd 'ala Kitab al-Mathal al-Sa'ir," said in his words. He said: The Imam, the memorizer (al-hafiz) Sharaf al-Din Abd al-Mu'min ibn Khalaf al-Dimyati, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him, recited to us from him:

Were it not for three, I would not fear my downfall, which is not as the youth of the slave said:
That I support monotheism and justice in every station, exerting my utmost effort;
And that I converse with Allah, enjoying a solitude sweeter than honey;
And that I rise up proudly against every base person with a sneering face.
For that I desire, not a young woman nor wine nor one with a shapely, full-bosomed figure.

﴿And said, "Indeed I am of the Muslims"﴾: The meaning is not that he uttered these words, but that he made Islam his creed. Just as you say, "This is the saying of al-Shafi'i," meaning his doctrine.

Ibn Abi Ablah and Ibrahim ibn Nuh, from Qutayba al-Mayyal, read "wa qala inni" with a single doubled nun; the majority read "inanni" with it and with the nun of protection (nun al-wiqaya).

Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi said: no condition was stipulated except "if Allah wills," so this is a refutation of those who say, "I am a Muslim, if Allah wills."

When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned that no one is better than the one who calls to Allah, He mentioned what follows from that of good character, and that the caller to Allah may be met with harshness by the one he calls, so he should be gentle with him and kind in conveying the good to him (p-498).

It was said: it was revealed concerning Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, who had been an enemy of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and then became a sincere ally.

Ibn Abbas said: "the good deed" is "there is no god but Allah," and "the evil deed" is polytheism (shirk). al-Kalbi said: the two calls to them.

al-Dahhak said: forbearance and foul speech. From Ali: love of the Messenger and his household and hatred of their enemies. It was said: patience and aversion.

It was said: tolerance and harshness. It was said: pardon and moderation. These are examples of the good and the evil, not a restrictive enumeration.

Since the good and the evil differ, He commanded that the evil be repelled with what is better, and this is for emphasis. He did not say, "Repel the evil with the good," because whoever finds it easy to repel with the better will find it easy to repel with the good. That is, when you do that, ﴿then he between whom and you is enmity﴾ becomes for you like a close friend, a loyal ally of sincere friendship. The "la" (لا) in His saying ﴿nor is the evil﴾ is an extra particle for emphasis, just as it is in His saying ﴿nor is the shade [equal to] the heat﴾ [Fatir 35:21], because "istawa" (to be equal) does not suffice with a single noun. The one of the good and the evil is a category, so its addition would not be like its addition in the previous aspect, for the meaning would become: "the good deeds are not equal," since they vary in themselves, "nor the evil deeds," because they too vary.

Ibn Atiyya said: "ka'anna" (as if) came for comparison, because the one who has enmity does not become a warm, loyal ally, but his outward appearance becomes good, so he is likened to the warm ally.

From Ibn Abbas: ﴿with that which is better﴾ means patience when angry, forbearance when ignorant, and pardon when wronged.

Mujahid and Ata' said: greeting at the time of meeting. End of quote. That is, it is the starting point of repelling with what is better, because it is confined to it.

Also from Mujahid: turn away from their harm. Abu Firas al-Hamdani said:

He wrongs me, and I bend, always greeting him with a face of welcome.
Nothing is better than one side turned toward the other side.

And none is granted it except those who are patient, and none is granted it except one of great fortune.

[Translation of the passage follows.]

**﴿وما يُلَقّاها﴾**: The pronoun refers to the act and the disposition, which is repelling evil with what is better. Talha ibn Musarrif and Ibn Kathir, in one transmission, read ﴿وما يُلَقّاها﴾ from al-mulaqah (encountering). The majority read it from al-taladdi (receiving). It is as if this noble trait is absent, so none encounters it or is granted it by God except one who is patient in acts of obedience, restraining himself from desires, and possessing a great share of the qualities of goodness. This is said by Ibn Abbas, and it is then praise. Or (ذُو حَظٍّ عَظِيمٍ) means a great share of the reward of the Hereafter, said by Qatada, and then it is a promise. It is also said: except one of intellect. And it is said: one of good character. He repeated ﴿وما يُلَقّاها﴾ to emphasise this beautiful and sublime act. It is also said that the pronoun in (يُلَقّاها) refers to Paradise.

Makki related: ﴿وما يُلَقّاها﴾ means the testimony that there is no god but God, but this is far-fetched.

When God commanded repelling evil with what is better, a Muslim may at times be inclined to respond to one who has wronged him with evil. So He commanded him, if this arises in him, to seek refuge in God, for that is a prick of Satan (نَزْغ الشَّيْطانِ, a prompting of Satan). The explanation of the like of this verse has already been given at the end of al-A'raf.

When God made clear that the best of deeds and words is the like of this verse, which is calling to God, He followed it with mention of the signs above and below, of His overpowering power, His perfect wisdom, and His decisive proof. He began with mention of the celestial matters, night and day, and He placed the mention of night first. It is said: as a reminder that darkness is an absence and light is an existence. The mention of the sun after the day is fitting, because it is the cause of its illumination and by it the world appears, and because it is more effective in illumination than the moon, and because the moon, as they say, derives its light from the light of the sun.

Then God forbade prostration to them both, and commanded prostration to the Creator, exalted is He.

Some people used to worship the sun, as is mentioned in the story of Bilqis and her people. The pronoun in (خَلَقَهُنَّ) refers to the night, the day, the sun and the moon.

Al-Zamakhshari said: because the rule for a plural of non-rational things is the rule of the feminine, i.e., feminine forms, one says: "al-aqlam, I sharpened them" and "bariytuhunna" (I sharpened them, feminine). He ended, meaning non-rational masculine nouns. He should have distinguished among the plural of paucity in this, for the more eloquent usage is that it is treated like the pronoun of the feminine singular: one says "al-ajdha'u inkasarat" (the trunks broke) in the most eloquent usage, and "al-judhu'u inkasarna" (the trunks broke, feminine plural) in the most eloquent usage.

What precedes in the verse is not a plural of paucity in a single form; rather, it mentions four items joined by conjunction, so they are placed in the position of a plural expressed by a single word.

Al-Zamakhshari also said: when He said ﴿ومِن آياتِهِ﴾ (and among His signs), they were in the sense of signs, so it was said ﴿خَلَقَهُنَّ﴾ (He created them, feminine plural). He ended, meaning: the sense is "the night, the day, the sun and the moon are among His signs," so the pronoun returns to the plural "signs" implied in the genitive. It is also said that it returns to the signs mentioned previously. It is also said that it returns to the sun and the moon, and the dual is a plural, and the plural of non-rational things takes the feminine; and since it is said "shumus" and "aqmar" (suns and moons), because they differ by days and nights, it is permissible for the pronoun to return in the plural.

Ibn Wahb and al-Shafi'i said: at ﴿يَسْأمُونَ﴾, and Abu Hanifa also held this view. Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar, Abu Wa'il, Bakr ibn Abdullah prostrated there, and likewise it is related from Masruq, al-Sulami, al-Nakha'i, Abu Salih and Ibn Sirin. He ended, summarized.

﴿فَإنِ اسْتَكْبَرُوا﴾ means: they magnified themselves, refusing to avoid what I forbade of prostrating to these two created, ordered beings, and to comply with what I commanded of prostrating to the Creator of them; for the angels, who are with God in noble rank and station, glorify Him above what does not befit His majesty, ﴿وهم لا يَسْأمُونَ﴾ means they do not weary of that. And they are better than you, while God is free of need of your worship and of theirs.

When He mentioned some of the celestial signs, He mentioned some of the terrestrial signs, saying: ﴿ومِن آياتِهِ أنَّكَ تَرى الأرْضَ خاشِعَةً﴾ meaning: dusty and effaced, as the poet said:

*And a stone-ring like the trunk of a pool, faded and humble.*

Humility (al-khushu') is borrowed for it, which is submission because of the drought, absence of vegetation and hardship of life that appear in it, unlike when it is verdant with plants, flowering and fruitful trees, for that is its life.

Al-Sudi said: (خاشِعَةً) means dead and dry. The discussion of ﴿فَإذا أنْزَلْنا عَلَيْها الماءَ اهْتَزَّتْ ورَبَتْ﴾ (then when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells) has already been given, both in interpretation and recitation, at the beginning of Surat al-Hajj.
