He said: "You have taken the matter to its extreme." They said: "Then what do you say?" He said: "They did not return to the worship of idols." End of quote.

﴿The angels descend upon them﴾: Mujahid and al-Suddi said: at death. Muqatil said: at the resurrection. It was also said: at death, in the grave, and at the resurrection. Here "an" (أنْ) is a particle that governs the imperfect verb (nasiba li-l-mudari'), meaning: "by the absence of your fear and your grief." This was said by al-Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa'.

al-Zamakhshari said: it has the meaning of "ay" (أيْ, that is), or it is the light form (mukhaffafa) of the heavy "inna," and its original form is "bi-annahu la takhafu," with the pronoun "ha'" being the pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n). End of quote. According to these two interpretations, the verb is in the jussive mood after the prohibitive "la" (لا). This is a general verse for every future concern and a complete consolation for every past loss. Therefore Mujahid said: "Do not fear" what you have power over, and ﴿nor grieve﴾ over what you have left behind of your worldly life.

Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: "Do not fear" the rejection of your reward, for it is accepted; "nor grieve" over your sins, for I shall forgive them for you.

In the reading of Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud), it is "la takhafu" (without "an"), meaning: ﴿the angels descend upon them﴾ saying, "Do not fear and do not grieve."

Since fear of what is expected of harm is greater than grief over what has been lost, He mentioned it first. Then, when security was established for them, they were given good news of what they would attain, namely entry into Paradise. Thus they obtained complete security and great joy concerning the good they would do.

﴿We are your allies (awliya')﴾: The apparent meaning is that this is from the speech of the angels, meaning they say to them. In the reading of Abdullah, it forms part of what was said before, meaning: "We were your allies in the world, and we are your allies in the Hereafter."

Since the allies (awliya') of the disbelievers are their companions from the devils, the allies of the believers are the angels.

al-Suddi said: "We are your guardians (hafaza) in the world, and your allies in the Hereafter." It was also said: ﴿We are your allies﴾ is from the speech of Allah, exalted is He, meaning allies in sufficiency and guidance. ﴿And for you therein﴾: the pronoun refers to the Hereafter, as Ibn Atiyya said. al-Hawfi said it refers to Paradise.

﴿What your souls desire﴾ of pleasures, ﴿and for you therein is what you call for﴾. Muqatil said: what you wish for. It was also said: what you want. Ibn Isa said: whatever you claim is yours, it is yours by the decree of your Lord. Ibn Atiyya said: what you request.

﴿As a hospitable gift (nuzulan) from a Forgiving, Merciful [One]﴾: "Nuzul" is the provision prepared for a guest (nazil), who is the visitor. Ibn Ata' said this, so "nuzulan" is then a circumstantial accusative (hal), meaning you are given that in the state of being a provision, not as a [mere] gift. Some have made it a verbal noun from "anzala."

It was also said that "nuzul" is the plural of "nazil," like "sharif" and "shurf," so it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state, meaning "descending/arriving," and the subject of the state is the pronoun in "yad'una." al-Hasan said: the meaning of "nuzulan" is "from Us." It was also said: a reward. Abu Haywa read it as "nuzlan" with the zay sukun.

Since His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, those who have said, "Our Lord is Allah," then remained steadfast﴾ has preceded, He mentioned the one who calls to that, saying: ﴿And who is better in speech than one who invites to Allah and does righteous deeds and says, "Indeed I am of the Muslims"?﴾ That is, no one is better in speech than the one who calls to the monotheism of Allah, does righteous deeds, and declares that he is among those who submit to the command of Allah and comply with Him. The apparent meaning is general for every caller to Allah, and al-Hasan, Muqatil, and a group held this general view. It was also said that it is specific: Ibn Abbas said it is the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who called to Islam, did righteous deeds between himself and his Lord, and made Islam a faith. He also said from him: they are the companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

Aisha, Qays ibn Abi Hazim, Ikrima, and Mujahid said: it was revealed concerning the muezzins (mu'adhdhinun). Their statement should be interpreted as meaning that they are included in the verse; otherwise, the surah in its entirety is Meccan without any disagreement. The call to prayer (adhan) was not in Mecca; it was legislated in Medina. The call to Allah is by calling to Islam, by fighting the disbelievers, and by restraining the oppressors.

Zayd ibn Ali said: he called to Allah by the sword, and this—Allah knows best—is what prompted him to rise with the sword against some of the oppressive rulers of the Banu Umayya.

This Zayd was a scholar of the Book of Allah, and I have come across a portion of his exegesis of the Book of Allah, and his delivering it to some of those who transmitted from him while he was imprisoned by Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik. It contains a great share of knowledge and citation of the speech of the Arabs. It is said that when he and his brother Muhammad al-Baqir debated, people gathered with inkwells, writing down what proceeded from them of knowledge. May Allah have mercy on them both and be pleased with them.

Abu al-Aliya said: ﴿and does righteous deeds﴾: he prayed between the adhan and the iqama. Ikrima said: he prayed and fasted. al-Kalbi said: he performed the obligatory duties. Mujahid said: it is general for everyone who combines these three: being a monotheist, holding the faith of Islam, acting in goodness, and calling to it. Their final destination is the rank of the knowledgeable who act, from among the people of justice (adl) and monotheism (tawhid), the callers to the religion of Islam. End of quote. He means by this the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school), who call themselves "the people of justice and monotheism," and this is found in their poetry, as Ibn Abi al-Hadid the Mu'tazili, author of the book "al-Falak al-Da'ir fi al-Radd 'ala Kitab al-Mathal al-Sa'ir," said in his words. He said: The Imam, the memorizer (al-hafiz) Sharaf al-Din Abd al-Mu'min ibn Khalaf al-Dimyati, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him, recited to us from him:

Were it not for three, I would not fear my downfall, which is not as the youth of the slave said:
That I support monotheism and justice in every station, exerting my utmost effort;
And that I converse with Allah, enjoying a solitude sweeter than honey;
And that I rise up proudly against every base person with a sneering face.
For that I desire, not a young woman nor wine nor one with a shapely, full-bosomed figure.

﴿And said, "Indeed I am of the Muslims"﴾: The meaning is not that he uttered these words, but that he made Islam his creed. Just as you say, "This is the saying of al-Shafi'i," meaning his doctrine.

Ibn Abi Ablah and Ibrahim ibn Nuh, from Qutayba al-Mayyal, read "wa qala inni" with a single doubled nun; the majority read "inanni" with it and with the nun of protection (nun al-wiqaya).

Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi said: no condition was stipulated except "if Allah wills," so this is a refutation of those who say, "I am a Muslim, if Allah wills."

When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned that no one is better than the one who calls to Allah, He mentioned what follows from that of good character, and that the caller to Allah may be met with harshness by the one he calls, so he should be gentle with him and kind in conveying the good to him (p-498).

It was said: it was revealed concerning Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, who had been an enemy of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and then became a sincere ally.

Ibn Abbas said: "the good deed" is "there is no god but Allah," and "the evil deed" is polytheism (shirk). al-Kalbi said: the two calls to them.

al-Dahhak said: forbearance and foul speech. From Ali: love of the Messenger and his household and hatred of their enemies. It was said: patience and aversion.

It was said: tolerance and harshness. It was said: pardon and moderation. These are examples of the good and the evil, not a restrictive enumeration.

Since the good and the evil differ, He commanded that the evil be repelled with what is better, and this is for emphasis. He did not say, "Repel the evil with the good," because whoever finds it easy to repel with the better will find it easy to repel with the good. That is, when you do that, ﴿then he between whom and you is enmity﴾ becomes for you like a close friend, a loyal ally of sincere friendship. The "la" (لا) in His saying ﴿nor is the evil﴾ is an extra particle for emphasis, just as it is in His saying ﴿nor is the shade [equal to] the heat﴾ [Fatir 35:21], because "istawa" (to be equal) does not suffice with a single noun. The one of the good and the evil is a category, so its addition would not be like its addition in the previous aspect, for the meaning would become: "the good deeds are not equal," since they vary in themselves, "nor the evil deeds," because they too vary.

Ibn Atiyya said: "ka'anna" (as if) came for comparison, because the one who has enmity does not become a warm, loyal ally, but his outward appearance becomes good, so he is likened to the warm ally.

From Ibn Abbas: ﴿with that which is better﴾ means patience when angry, forbearance when ignorant, and pardon when wronged.

Mujahid and Ata' said: greeting at the time of meeting. End of quote. That is, it is the starting point of repelling with what is better, because it is confined to it.

Also from Mujahid: turn away from their harm. Abu Firas al-Hamdani said:

He wrongs me, and I bend, always greeting him with a face of welcome.
Nothing is better than one side turned toward the other side.

And none is granted it except those who are patient, and none is granted it except one of great fortune.

[Translation of the passage follows.]

**﴿وما يُلَقّاها﴾**: The pronoun refers to the act and the disposition, which is repelling evil with what is better. Talha ibn Musarrif and Ibn Kathir, in one transmission, read ﴿وما يُلَقّاها﴾ from al-mulaqah (encountering). The majority read it from al-taladdi (receiving). It is as if this noble trait is absent, so none encounters it or is granted it by God except one who is patient in acts of obedience, restraining himself from desires, and possessing a great share of the qualities of goodness. This is said by Ibn Abbas, and it is then praise. Or (ذُو حَظٍّ عَظِيمٍ) means a great share of the reward of the Hereafter, said by Qatada, and then it is a promise. It is also said: except one of intellect. And it is said: one of good character. He repeated ﴿وما يُلَقّاها﴾ to emphasise this beautiful and sublime act. It is also said that the pronoun in (يُلَقّاها) refers to Paradise.

Makki related: ﴿وما يُلَقّاها﴾ means the testimony that there is no god but God, but this is far-fetched.

When God commanded repelling evil with what is better, a Muslim may at times be inclined to respond to one who has wronged him with evil. So He commanded him, if this arises in him, to seek refuge in God, for that is a prick of Satan (نَزْغ الشَّيْطانِ, a prompting of Satan). The explanation of the like of this verse has already been given at the end of al-A'raf.

When God made clear that the best of deeds and words is the like of this verse, which is calling to God, He followed it with mention of the signs above and below, of His overpowering power, His perfect wisdom, and His decisive proof. He began with mention of the celestial matters, night and day, and He placed the mention of night first. It is said: as a reminder that darkness is an absence and light is an existence. The mention of the sun after the day is fitting, because it is the cause of its illumination and by it the world appears, and because it is more effective in illumination than the moon, and because the moon, as they say, derives its light from the light of the sun.

Then God forbade prostration to them both, and commanded prostration to the Creator, exalted is He.

Some people used to worship the sun, as is mentioned in the story of Bilqis and her people. The pronoun in (خَلَقَهُنَّ) refers to the night, the day, the sun and the moon.

Al-Zamakhshari said: because the rule for a plural of non-rational things is the rule of the feminine, i.e., feminine forms, one says: "al-aqlam, I sharpened them" and "bariytuhunna" (I sharpened them, feminine). He ended, meaning non-rational masculine nouns. He should have distinguished among the plural of paucity in this, for the more eloquent usage is that it is treated like the pronoun of the feminine singular: one says "al-ajdha'u inkasarat" (the trunks broke) in the most eloquent usage, and "al-judhu'u inkasarna" (the trunks broke, feminine plural) in the most eloquent usage.

What precedes in the verse is not a plural of paucity in a single form; rather, it mentions four items joined by conjunction, so they are placed in the position of a plural expressed by a single word.

Al-Zamakhshari also said: when He said ﴿ومِن آياتِهِ﴾ (and among His signs), they were in the sense of signs, so it was said ﴿خَلَقَهُنَّ﴾ (He created them, feminine plural). He ended, meaning: the sense is "the night, the day, the sun and the moon are among His signs," so the pronoun returns to the plural "signs" implied in the genitive. It is also said that it returns to the signs mentioned previously. It is also said that it returns to the sun and the moon, and the dual is a plural, and the plural of non-rational things takes the feminine; and since it is said "shumus" and "aqmar" (suns and moons), because they differ by days and nights, it is permissible for the pronoun to return in the plural.

﴿إنْ كُنْتُمْ إيّاهُ تَعْبُدُونَ﴾ means: if you are monotheists, not associators.

The prostration, according to al-Shafi'i, is at (تَعْبُدُونَ) (you worship), and this is the transmission of Masruq from Abdullah, because the word "prostration" is mentioned before it. According to Abu Hanifa it is at ﴿لا يَسْأمُونَ﴾ (they do not tire), because it completes the meaning. In al-Tahrir: Ali and Ibn Mas'ud used to prostrate at (تَعْبُدُونَ). Ibn Wahb and al-Shafi'i said: at ﴿يَسْأمُونَ﴾, and Abu Hanifa also held this view. Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar, Abu Wa'il, Bakr ibn Abdullah prostrated there, and likewise it is related from Masruq, al-Sulami, al-Nakha'i, Abu Salih and Ibn Sirin. He ended, summarized.

﴿فَإنِ اسْتَكْبَرُوا﴾ means: they magnified themselves, refusing to avoid what I forbade of prostrating to these two created, ordered beings, and to comply with what I commanded of prostrating to the Creator of them; for the angels, who are with God in noble rank and station, glorify Him above what does not befit His majesty, ﴿وهم لا يَسْأمُونَ﴾ means they do not weary of that. And they are better than you, while God is free of need of your worship and of theirs.

When He mentioned some of the celestial signs, He mentioned some of the terrestrial signs, saying: ﴿ومِن آياتِهِ أنَّكَ تَرى الأرْضَ خاشِعَةً﴾ meaning: dusty and effaced, as the poet said:

*And a stone-ring like the trunk of a pool, faded and humble.*

Humility (al-khushu') is borrowed for it, which is submission because of the drought, absence of vegetation and hardship of life that appear in it, unlike when it is verdant with plants, flowering and fruitful trees, for that is its life.

Al-Sudi said: (خاشِعَةً) means dead and dry. The discussion of ﴿فَإذا أنْزَلْنا عَلَيْها الماءَ اهْتَزَّتْ ورَبَتْ﴾ (then when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells) has already been given, both in interpretation and recitation, at the beginning of Surat al-Hajj.

﴿إنَّ الَّذِي أحْياها لَمُحْيِي المَوْتى﴾: He who gives it life is surely the giver of life to the dead, returning souls to bodies. ﴿إنَّهُ عَلى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ﴾: nothing overcomes Him, on anything whatever upon which His will is set.

When God had shown that calling people to the religion of God is among the greatest acts of devotion (p-500), and that this is achieved by presenting the proofs of tawhid (the oneness of God), justice, and resurrection, He returned to warning those who dispute these signs and argue against them. He said: ﴿Indeed, those who deviate concerning Our verses are not hidden from Us. Is one who is thrown into the Fire better, or one who comes secure on the Day of Resurrection? Do as you wish; indeed, He is Seeing of what you do.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the Reminder when it came to them [will be exposed]. And indeed, it is a Book of might.﴾ ﴿Falsehood cannot approach it from before it or behind it; it is a revelation from the Wise, the Praiseworthy.﴾ ﴿Nothing is said to you except what was said to the messengers before you. Indeed, your Lord is Possessor of forgiveness and Possessor of painful punishment.﴾ ﴿And if We had made it a non-Arabic Qur'an, they would have said, "Why were its verses not explained in detail? Is it non-Arabic and Arabic?" Say: "It is, for those who believe, guidance and healing. And those who do not believe, in their ears is deafness, and it is blindness for them. Those are called from a distant place."﴾ ﴿And We had given Moses the Book, but it was disputed about. And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord, it would have been judged between them. And indeed, they are in doubt about it, disquieting.﴾ ﴿Whoever does righteousness, it is for his own soul; and whoever does evil, it is against it. And your Lord is not ever unjust to the servants.﴾

When God mentioned that those who deviate concerning His verses are not hidden from Him, and that those who disbelieve in the Qur'an are such that their obstinacy and denial are evident, and their saying, "Why was it not revealed in the language of non-Arabs?", He said: ﴿And if We had made it a non-Arabic Qur'an﴾, meaning one that is not clear and whose meanings are not understood by them because it is in the language of non-Arabs or a language other than Arabic, they would not have abandoned objection, and they would say: ﴿Why were its verses not explained to us﴾, meaning, made clear and elucidated so that we may understand them.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿a'jamiyyun﴾ with an interrogative hamza, followed by a long vowel which is the hamza of a'jamiyy. Its standard reduction is tashil bayn bayn (an intermediate softening of the hamza). Al-Akhawan (Hamzah and al-Kisa'i), al-A'mash, and Hafs read it with two hamzas, meaning, as a rejecting question: "Is it a non-Arabic Qur'an and an Arab messenger?" or "a non-Arabic Qur'an and an Arab addressee?" Ibn Jubayr interpreted the phrase ﴿a'jamiyy﴾ as meaning: "We are Arabs, what have we to do with non-Arabic speech?" Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "Because they deny that, and they say: 'Why was it not made clear, a non-Arabic and Arabic mixture? This is not good.'" End of quote.

This division is not valid, because it refers to the Qur'an, whereas what they said is what God's words ﴿And if We had made it a non-Arabic Qur'an﴾ indicated, namely their suggestion that it be non-Arabic; they did not suggest that the Qur'an be both non-Arabic and Arabic. Al-Hasan, Abu al-Aswad, al-Jahdari, Salam, al-Dahhak, Ibn 'Abbas, and Ibn 'Amir (with a variant from them both) read ﴿a'jamiyyun wa 'arabiyy﴾ without interrogation and with a sukun on the 'ayn. It was said that its meaning is: they said, "'Ujmah and i'rab (non-Arabic and Arabic inflection), indeed this is anomalous."

Ibn Jubayr said its meaning is: "Why was it not distinguished into two parts, so that part of it is non-Arabic (a'jami), understood by non-Arabs, and part of it is Arabic, understood by Arabs?"

The author of al-Lawami' said: When they said, "Why have its verses not been distinguished?" (﴿لَوْلا فُصِّلَتْ آياتُهُ﴾), they repeated the statement a second time, saying "a'jami," and the subject was omitted, meaning: "It is non-Arabic," referring to the Qur'an, or the speech, or something similar, while "the one who brought it," or "the Messenger," is Arabic. As if they were denying that.

Amr ibn Maymun recited "a'jami" with a interrogative hamzah and a fatha on the ayn, meaning: if the Qur'an had come in a form that was [already] present, they would have been obstinate, because they do not seek the truth.

The author of al-Lawami' said: "'Ajami" means one attributed to the non-Arabs (al-'Ajam), and the yā' is the true relative suffix. But when the ayn is vowelled with sukun, it means one who is not eloquent, and the yā' in it is in the form of a relative suffix but not in its meaning; it is like the yā' of kursiyy (chair) and bukhtiyy (Bactrian camel). And Allah knows best. End of quotation.

It is not like the yā' of kursiyy, upon which the word is built; nor is the yā' of a'jamiyy one upon which the word is built. The Arabs say: "rajul a'jam" and "rajul a'jamiyy," so the yā' is a relative suffix indicating intensification of the attribute, like ahmariyy and duwariyy, intensifying ahmar and duwar.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: how can 'Arabi' be intended to refer to the people to whom it was sent, who are the Arab nation? I say: it is as it should be in denouncing the denier, were he to see a non-Arabic book written to a people of the Arabs, saying: 'A book in non-Arabic, while its addressee is Arab?' Because the denunciation is directed at the incongruity between the state of the book and the state of its addressee, not at whether the addressee is one person or a group. Therefore it must be kept to the purpose for which it was brought, and not connected to another purpose.

Do you not see that you say, when you have seen a long garment on a short woman: 'The garment is long and the wearer is short'? If you said, 'The wearer [feminine] is short,' you would have produced a solecism and superfluous speech, because the speech did not concern the masculinity or femininity of the wearer, but a purpose beyond them." End of quotation. It is good, except that it contains excess, in keeping with his habit of loving ornate display and verbosity.

﴿Say: it is﴾, that is, the Qur'an, ﴿for those who believe, a guidance and a healing﴾. Guidance means direction to the truth; healing means for what is in the breasts of doubt and suspicion.

It is apparent that ﴿And those who do not believe﴾ is a subject, and ﴿in their ears is a deafness﴾ is the place of the predicate.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "[It is] ﴿in their ears is a deafness﴾ with the subject omitted. When he informed that it is guidance and healing for the believers, he informed that it is deafness and dumbness in their ears, meaning the unbelievers, and there is no need to posit an implied 'huwa'; the sentence is complete without it. He informed that in their ears is deafness from hearing.

Then he informed that it is blindness upon them, preventing them from seeing its wisdom, contemplating its meanings, and reflecting upon its verses. He used the expression 'upon them,' which indicates the dominance of blindness over them, and for the believers he used the lam, which indicates exclusivity."

That ﴿and those who﴾ is in the genitive position, conjoined to His saying ﴿for those who believe﴾, the estimate being: "and for those who do not believe is a deafness in their ears" — is a forced grammatical analysis, being conjunction over two governors, and in grammar there are many positions on it, though the well-known view is to forbid it.

Al-Jumhur read ʿaman with a fatha on the mim, with tanwin, as a verbal noun of ʿamiya. Ibn ʿAmr, Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn al-Zubayr, Muawiya ibn Abi Sufyan, Amr ibn al-As, and Ibn Hurmuz read it with a kasra on the mim and tanwin.

Yaʿqub al-Qari and Abu Hatim said: "We do not know whether they put tanwin or made the yā' fatha, as a past verb, without tanwin"; this was transmitted by Amr ibn Dinar and Sulayman ibn Qutayba from Ibn ʿAbbas. It is apparent that the pronoun in ﴿and it upon them﴾ returns to the Qur'an, and it has been said that it returns to the deafness.

﴿Those﴾ is a reference to those who do not believe; and whoever makes it a predicate, [the reason being] that the unbelievers were the referent of the demonstrative.

﴿They are called from a far place﴾. It has been said this is literal. Al-Dahhak said: they are called out for their disbelief and the ugliness of their deeds, by their most abhorrent names, from a distance, so that the people of the gathering hear it, and their disgrace is magnified and their affliction is compounded. ʿAli and Mujahid said: it is a metaphor for their scant understanding; he likened them to a man who is called from a distance, who hears a sound but does not grasp its details or meanings. The people of lexicography relate that it is said to one who does not understand: "You are called from a far place," meaning, as if he is called from a distant place, so he neither hears the call nor understands it. Al-Naqqash related: as if they are called from the sky.

﴿And We certainly gave Musa the Book﴾. This is consolation for the Messenger regarding the fact that his people were in disagreement about what he brought of the Reminder. He mentioned that Musa, peace be upon him, was given the Book, which is the Torah; then there was disagreement about it. The explanation of this verse was already given at the end of Surah Hud, and the discussion of the parallel of ﴿And your Lord is not at all unjust to the servants﴾ in His saying in Surah al-Hajj: ﴿Indeed Allah is not unjust to the servants﴾ [al-Hajj: 10].

When God had shown that calling people to the religion of God is among the greatest acts of devotion (p-500), and that this is achieved by presenting the proofs of tawhid (the oneness of God), justice, and resurrection, He returned to warning those who dispute these signs and argue against them. He said: ﴿Indeed, those who deviate concerning Our verses are not hidden from Us. Is one who is thrown into the Fire better, or one who comes secure on the Day of Resurrection? Do as you wish; indeed, He is Seeing of what you do.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the Reminder when it came to them [will be exposed]. And indeed, it is a Book of might.﴾ ﴿Falsehood cannot approach it from before it or behind it; it is a revelation from the Wise, the Praiseworthy.﴾ ﴿Nothing is said to you except what was said to the messengers before you. Indeed, your Lord is Possessor of forgiveness and Possessor of painful punishment.﴾ ﴿And if We had made it a non-Arabic Qur'an, they would have said, "Why were its verses not explained in detail? Is it non-Arabic and Arabic?" Say: "It is, for those who believe, guidance and healing. And those who do not believe, in their ears is deafness, and it is blindness for them. Those are called from a distant place."﴾ ﴿And We had given Moses the Book, but it was disputed about. And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord, it would have been judged between them. Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 41, verse 47–54:

﴿To Him is referred the knowledge of the Hour. No fruit emerges from its sheaths, nor does any female conceive or give birth except with His knowledge. On the Day He calls out to them, "Where are My partners?" they will say, "We have informed You that none of us is a witness."﴾ ﴿And lost from them will be what they used to invoke before, and they will be certain that there is no escape for them.﴾ ﴿Man does not tire of asking for good, but if evil touches him, he is despairing and hopeless.﴾ ﴿And if We let him taste mercy from Us after adversity has touched him, he will surely say, "This is mine, and I do not think the Hour will ever come. And if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely have with Him the best reward." So We will inform those who disbelieved of what they did, and We will surely make them taste a severe punishment.﴾ ﴿And when We bestow favor upon man, he turns away and distances himself, but when evil touches him, he is one of lengthy supplication.﴾ ﴿Say, "Have you considered: if this is from Allah and you have disbelieved in it, who is more astray than one who is in extreme opposition?"﴾ ﴿We will show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves until it becomes clear to them that it is the truth. Is it not sufficient that your Lord is, over all things, a Witness?﴾ ﴿Unquestionably, they are in doubt about the meeting with their Lord. Unquestionably, He is all-encompassing of all things.﴾.

When He, the Exalted, mentioned "Whoever does righteousness [benefits his own soul]" [Fussilat: 46], etc., this indicated the recompense on the Day of Resurrection. As if a questioner said: "When is that?" It was said: "None knows it except Allah, and whoever is asked about it does not have knowledge of its specific time; rather, that is referred to Allah."

Then He mentioned the breadth of His knowledge and its relation to what none knows except Him, the Exalted.

Abu Ja'far, al-A'raj, Shayba, Qatada, and al-Hasan (with a variant from him), and Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir (in a non-transmitted reading, i.e., the clear one), and al-Mufaddal, Hafs, and Ibn Miqsam read: ﴿min thamarātin﴾ in the plural. The rest of the Seven, and al-Hasan in the narration of Talha, and al-A'mash read it in the singular.

Since what emerges from the sheaths of the tree, and what the females carry and give birth to, is the bringing into existence of things after non-existence, it is appropriate that it be mentioned together with the knowledge of the Hour, since in that is evidence of the Resurrection, being a restoration after annihilation. It is also appropriate to mention the states of the polytheists on that Day and their questioning in the manner of rebuke, so He said: ﴿And on the Day He calls out to them, "Where are My partners?"﴾, i.e., those whom you attributed to Me and claimed to be partners of Mine. In this is mockery of them and reproach.

The pronoun in ﴿yunādīhim﴾ is general to everyone who worshipped other than Allah, so the worshippers of idols are included in it.

﴿Qālū ādhannāka﴾, i.e., "We informed You." The poet said:

"Asmā' informed us of her separation, / many a dweller tires of his dwelling."

Ibn 'Abbas said: "We made You hear," as if he deemed the informing of Allah improbable, because the people of the Resurrection know that Allah knows things with necessary knowledge, so informing Him is impossible in His regard. Apparently the pronoun in ﴿qālū﴾ refers to those being called, since they are the ones addressed.

(﴿Mā minnā﴾) — none of us today — and we have seen and heard. He is witness that You have a partner; rather, we are monotheists for You, and none of us sees them, because they have strayed from them and their gods have strayed from them; they do not see them at the moment of rebuke. It was also said: the pronoun in ﴿qālū﴾ refers to the partners, i.e., the partners said: "None of us is a witness to what they attributed to us of polytheism." And ﴿ādhannāka﴾ is suspended, because it has the meaning of informing. The clause ﴿mā minnā min shahīd﴾ is in the position of the object. Regarding the suspension of the verb "a'lam" (I know) we have seen a difference of opinion, and the correct view is that it is heard from the speech of the Arabs. Apparently their saying "ādhannāka" is performative, like your saying "I swear I will strike Zayd," even though it is a prior report; so the repetition of the question is a rebuke to them.

﴿And lost from them will be what they used to invoke before﴾, i.e., they forgot what they used to say in the world and invoke from the gods; or ﴿and lost from them﴾, i.e., their idols perished and vanished, so they found from them no help nor intercession; ﴿and they were certain﴾, i.e., they became sure. Al-Suddi said: ﴿mā lahum min maḥīs﴾ means: no escape or evasion from the punishment.

Apparently ﴿ẓannū﴾ is suspended, and the negated clause is in the position of the two objects of ﴿ẓannū﴾.

It was also said: the speech is complete at ﴿ẓannū﴾, i.e., it became more probable to them that their saying ﴿mā minnā min shahīd﴾ would be a means of deliverance for them, or a matter they use to disguise. The clause after that is a new sentence, i.e., there will be for them a refuge, or a place of escape.

﴿Man does not tire of asking for good﴾: these verses were revealed concerning disbelievers — it was said: concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira; it was said: concerning 'Utba ibn Rabi'a — and many Muslims also share in the description of its first part: from asking for good, i.e., from seeking abundance and blessing. ﴿Du'ā'﴾ is a verbal noun in the annexed form with the object. 'Abdullah read: ﴿min du'ā'in bil-khayr﴾, with a "bi" governing "khayr," and the subject of the verbal noun is omitted, its estimated form being: "from a supplication for good." ﴿Wa-in massahu al-sharr﴾, i.e., poverty and hardship, ﴿fa-ya'ūs﴾, i.e., he is then despairing, hopeless; and it came with both in intensive forms. Yaʾs is a quality of the heart, which is to cut off one's hope of good; qunūt is that the traces of despair appear upon him, so he shrinks and breaks. He began with the form of the heart, because it is the one that is apparently effective in the outward appearance of breaking.

﴿And if We let him taste mercy from Us﴾: He called the blessing "mercy," since it is among the effects of Allah's mercy.

﴿After adversity had touched him﴾, i.e., by my effort and striving, and he does not see that it is from Allah; or "this is mine," it will not depart from me.

﴿And I do not think the Hour will be established﴾, i.e., we think we will not be resurrected, and that what the messengers brought of that is not real, as He, the Exalted, said quoting them: ﴿If we think only a supposition, and we are not certain﴾ [al-Jathiya: 32].

﴿And if I am returned to my Lord﴾: even if it is as the messengers reported, ﴿I surely have with Him﴾, i.e., with Allah, ﴿the best (lal-husnā)﴾: i.e., the best state of honor and blessing, as He bestowed upon me in the world. They emphasized this with an oath, and by placing ﴿lī ʿindahu﴾ before the subject of "inna," and the emphatic lam enters upon it too; and with the form "al-husnā" the superlative "al-aḥsan" is made feminine. They did not say "la-l-ḥasanata," i.e., the good state. Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn ʿAli ibn Abi Talib — may Allah be pleased with them — said: "The disbeliever has two wishes: in this world, this one: ﴿Indeed I have with Him the best﴾; and in the Hereafter: ﴿Would that I were dust﴾ [al-Naba': 40]."

﴿So We will inform those who disbelieved of what they did﴾ among the evil deeds; and that is a metonymy for their recompense for their evil deeds.

﴿And We will surely make them taste a severe punishment﴾ in opposition to ﴿Indeed I have with Him﴾. He described the punishment as "severe" (ghalīẓ) as a metonymy for its intensity.

﴿And when We bestow favor﴾: the discussion of the parallel of this clause has already been given in (Subḥān), except that at the end of that is ﴿kāna yaʾūsan﴾ [al-Isra': 83] and at the end of this is ﴿fa-dhū duʿāʾin ʿarīḍ﴾: i.e., he is then one of supplication for the removal of evil from himself and the lifting of his harm.

The Arabs use "length" and "breadth" for abundance. It is said: "So-and-so extended in wrongdoing" and "he went to lengths in supplication" when he increased it, i.e., he is one of humble entreaty and pleading.

In this verse He mentioned a kind of human rebellion: when Allah afflicts him with a blessing that makes him insolent, and when evil touches him he implores Allah and humbles himself.

﴿Say: Have you considered, if it is﴾, i.e., the Qur'an, ﴿from Allah﴾: he presented it in the form of supposition, though it is from Allah without doubt, but it descended addressing them in their own mode of speech. The pronoun in ﴿arā'aytum﴾ refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh. It has been stated that the meaning of "arā'aytum" is: inform me of your condition, ﴿if it is﴾ this Qur'an ﴿from Allah﴾, and you disbelieved in it and opposed in following it.

"Who is more astray among you," since you are the opponents in it, the ones who turn away from it, and the mockers of Allah's signs.

It has been stated that this "arā'aytum" takes an object, either mentioned or omitted, and a second object which is usually an interrogative clause. The first object is omitted, its estimated form being: "Have you considered yourselves?" and the second is the interrogative clause, since its meaning is: "Who is more astray among you, O disbelievers, since your end is destruction in this world and the Hereafter."

Then He threatened them with what is certain to occur without doubt, saying: ﴿We will show them Our signs in the horizons﴾.

Abu al-Minhal, al-Suddi, and a group said: this is a threat to the disbelievers with what Allah will open to His Messenger of the regions around Mecca, and elsewhere in the land, such as Khaybar.

﴿And within themselves﴾: he meant by it the conquest of Mecca, and that contained the report of the unseen, and it occurred as he reported.

Al-Dahhak and Qatada said: ﴿in the horizons﴾: what befell the deniers' nations in the regions of the earth in former times; ﴿and within themselves﴾: the Day of Badr.

'Ata' and Ibn Zayd said: in the horizons of the heavens, meaning the signs in the sun, the moon, the winds, and other things; ﴿and within themselves﴾: the lesson of man in his body, his senses, his strange creation, and his gradual development in the belly and the like.

These two statements alert us away from the wording "We will show them," because the destruction of the earlier denying nations, and the signs of the sun and moon and other things, were all already visible to them; so the first statement is more probable.

Al-Zamakhshari took up this view and appended to it, saying: he means what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, facilitated for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and for the caliphs after him and the supporters of his religion, in the horizons of the world, the lands of East and West generally, and in the region of the Arabs specifically, of conquests such as had not been facilitated for anyone among the creatures of the earth before them, and of prevailing over the tyrants and Chosroes, and of the few overcoming the many, and of the weak subduing the strong, and of His bringing about through their hands matters outside what is customary and breaking habit, and of spreading the call of Islam in the inhabited regions and extending its state to their farthest parts.

Investigation will show you, in the histories and written books, in the scenes of its people and their days, wonders; you will not see any event of theirs except as a sign of Allah's signs and a verse of His verses, by which the soul is strengthened, faith increases, and it becomes clear that the religion of Islam is the religion of truth, from which none turns away except a stubborn, wicked person deceiving himself. End of what we wrote, restricting ourselves to it.

﴿Until it becomes clear to them that it﴾, i.e., the Qur'an, and what it contains of the law, is the truth, since it occurred in accordance with what it reported of the unseen. And (﴿bi-rabbika﴾): the "bi" is extra; the estimate is: "Is it not sufficient for you, or for them, that your Lord..." and ﴿annahu ʿalā kulli shayʾin shahīd﴾ is a substitute for ﴿rabbika﴾.

As-Sulami and al-Hasan read "fī murbatin" with a damma on the mim. His encompassing of things is His knowledge of them in totality and in detail; so He will recompense them for their disbelief and their doubt about the meeting with their Lord.

When He, the Exalted, mentioned "Whoever does righteousness [benefits his own soul]" [Fussilat: 46], etc., this indicated the recompense on the Day of Resurrection. Then He mentioned the breadth of His knowledge and its relation to what none knows except Him, the Exalted.
